paragraphs.text: In the primary analysis, the proportion of patients who experienced a grade 3 + AE or SAE attributed to FP or irinotecan during the first three treatment cycles was lower in the variant carriers with genotype-guided treatment compared to standard treatment (12.5% vs. 50.7%, OR: 0.15; 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 0.03–0.68, Table 2, Fig. 1) overall and in variant carriers receiving genotype-guided FP (Table 2). None of the additional variables including sex, cancer type, DPD activity score, or regimen type were associated with toxicity risk in the conditional logistic regression model (data not shown). paragraphs.section: Comparison of AEs between genotype-guided and standard treatment
paragraphs.text: Of the 16 patients who received genotype-guided treatment, six (37.5%) had a dose escalation for their second or third treatment cycle. Five were DPD IMs who initiated FP at ~50% of the standard starting dose (Supplementary Table 3). All five patients tolerated the received dose escalation, which ranged from 62–100% of the standard dose. Additionally, one UGT1A1 PM who initiated irinotecan with a 50% dose reduction tolerated an increase to 75% of the standard dose.

paragraphs.section: Identification of variant carriers with standard treatment
paragraphs.text: Variant carriers who received standard treatment were then matched with the variant carriers in the genotype-guided group by DPD or UGT1A1 phenotype, chemotherapy regimen (i.e., chemotherapy agent and monotherapy or combination therapy, Supplementary Table 1), and age at time of treatment (+/− 10 years). For matching, the patient’s DPD phenotype was classified as an intermediate metabolizer (IM) or poor metabolizer (PM) according to the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) DPD activity score (Supplementary Table S2) [1]. Patients with homozygous or compound homozygous UGT1A1 variant genotypes were considered UGT1A1 PM per CPIC definitions [14].

A total of 91 subjects were included in this study, including 16 patients with genotype-guided treatment and 75 matched subjects with standard treatment (median (range) of 4.5 (1–9) standard treatment subjects matched to each genotype-guided subject). Demographics of the included patients are summarized in Table 1. Twelve (75%) were DPD IM who received genotype-guided FP and were matched with 56 DPD IM (74.7%) patients with standard treatment, while four (25%) were UGT1A1 PM who received genotype-guided irinotecan and were matched to 19 (25.3%) UGT1A1 PM subjects with standard treatment. paragraphs.text: While direct comparisons with historical cohorts are limited by differences in patient populations and supportive care over time, the incidences of severe neutropenia (36.1%) and diarrhea (17.0%) in our FOLFIRI-3 cohort did not exceed the rates generally reported in landmark trials of standard FOLFIRI-1 [2,3,4]. However, given the added logistical burden of a Day 3 irinotecan administration, this baseline safety profile alone does not justify the routine adoption of FOLFIRI-3 for all unselected mCRC patients. [PMID 42742701] (Archives of toxicology, 2026) Combined immune modulation reveals carbamazepine-associated CD8+ T cell-dependent skin inflammation in HLA-A*31:01 knock-in mice. Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles are among the strongest genetic risk factors for idiosyncratic drug toxicity. HLA-A*31:01 is a risk factor for carbamazepine (CBZ)-induced delayed drug hypersensitivity, yet allele carriage alone is insufficient for disease development. CD8+ T cells are implicated in these reactions; however, their activation mechanism remains unclear. Using HLA-A*31:01 knock-in (A31-KI) mice, we investigated whether CBZ exposure elicited CD8+ T-cell responses in vivo. The mice received CBZ for 7 days by oral administration (300 mg/kg/day) and auricular application (25 mg/kg/day). CBZ alone did not induce clear CD8+ T-cell activation. Under CD4+ T-cell depletion, CBZ markedly increased programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) expression in CD44highCD62Llow CD8+ T cells, suggesting PD-1-mediated restraint of CBZ-responsive activation. Subsequent PD-1 blockade enhanced CD8+ T-cell activation in auricular lymph nodes and induced skin inflammation with elevated serum thymus and activation-regulated chemokine; both were attenuated by CD8+ T-cell depletion. To clarify how CBZ activated CD8+ T cells, we performed ex vivo analyses using splenocytes. CBZ (50 µM) induced proliferation of CD44highCD8+ T cells, whereas this response was absent in purified CD8+ T-cell cultures and reduced by HLA class I and costimulatory blockade, supporting an antigen-presenting cell-dependent mechanism. Collectively, CBZ can activate CD8+ T cells; however, this response is restrained and remains latent. When immune control is disrupted, particularly in an HLA-A*31:01-bearing host, the response can progress to a CD8+ T cell-dependent inflammatory phenotype. Thus, A31-KI mice provide an in vivo platform for understanding CBZ-associated idiosyncratic toxicity and pathogenesis.

The clinical spectrum ranges from mild symptoms to severe cases associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Prolonged latency and clinical variability often result in delayed diagnosis, thereby increasing the risk of relapse upon re‐exposure. To ensure accurate diagnosis, structured tools such as the Registry of Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions (RegiSCAR) system are widely used, applying a two‐step framework with separate inclusion and validation (scoring) criteria. Diagnostic classification is based on the validation score, and importantly, rash is not mandatory; different combinations of clinical and laboratory features are allowed, reflecting the heterogeneity of DRESS [2]. The RegiSCAR score facilitates standardized diagnosis, supports the assessment of disease severity, and informs clinical decision‐making [3]. Notably, RegiSCAR provides a structured framework for diagnosis, although it does not by itself definitively establish drug causality [2, 3].
Early recognition and prompt withdrawal of the culprit drug are therefore essential. However, identifying the culprit drug remains particularly challenging, especially in patients exposed to multiple drugs concurrently [1].
In vitro tests, such as the lymphocyte transformation test (LTT) and the enzyme‐linked immunospot assay (ELISpot), are often recommended before in vivo tests, as in vivo tests carry a risk of systemic hypersensitivity reactions that may lead to disease flare or relapse. However, the diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of these in vitro tests remain incompletely validated [4, 5, 6]. Furthermore, they are primarily employed in research settings and are not routinely available in all clinical centers.
When in vitro tests are negative or unavailable, patch testing (PT) carries a relatively low risk of systemic reactions and may be considered after complete resolution of the acute phase in selected cases, especially in multidrug‐exposed patients. It may provide supportive information for identifying the culprit drug or assessing potential cross‐reactivity [6]. However, the diagnostic sensitivity of PT in DRESS is variable and generally limited, with reported positivity rates of approximately 50% at best in some studies. Because of the limited sensitivity of PT in DRESS, drug provocation testing (DPT) cannot be recommended solely based on a negative test result [7, 8].

paragraphs.text: Among 50 patients, 38 had SDH and 10 had MDHS, while two patients remained unclassified. Compared with SDH, MDHS patients had a significantly higher median RegiSCAR score (7 [6–8]) than SDH patients (6 [6–8]) (p < 0.001). Facial edema (p < 0.001) and lymphadenopathy (p = 0.042) were more common in MDHS. MDHS was also associated with a higher frequency of relevant HLA risk alleles (p = 0.038), including HLA‐B*58:01 (allopurinol), HLA‐A*31:01 (carbamazepine), HLA‐B*13:02 (levofloxacin) and HLA‐A*24:02 (lamotrigine), all previously reported to be associated with drug‐specific DRESS.

LTT and PT contributed to the identification of MDHS in our cohort; however, as not all patients underwent both tests, no direct comparison between the methods was possible. All affected patients carried HLA alleles linked to at least one culprit drug. Two patients had risk alleles associated with different drugs across two distinct DRESS episodes: one with HLA‐B*58:01 and HLA‐B*13:02 (allopurinol and levofloxacin) and another with HLA‐A*31:01 and HLA‐A*24:02 (carbamazepine and lamotrigine).

HLA risk alleles were identified in 11 alleles across 10 patients, including HLA‐B*58:01 (allopurinol, n = 3), HLA‐A*31:01 (carbamazepine, n = 2), HLA‐B*13:02 (levofloxacin, n = 2), HLA‐A*24:02 (lamotrigine, n = 1), HLA‐Cw*04:01 (antituberculosis drugs, n = 1), HLA‐A*32:01 (vancomycin, n = 1), and HLA‐A*02:06 (bendamustine, n = 1).

In the study, HLA genotyping confirmed several known risk alleles: HLA‐A*31:01 with carbamazepine‐induced DRESS, HLA‐A*24:02 with lamotrigine‐induced DRESS, and HLA‐B*13:02 with levofloxacin‐induced DRESS, consistent with previous studies [40, 41, 42]. HLA‐B*58:01 was present in allopurinol‐induced cases, reaffirming its established link, particularly among patients with renal impairment [43]. Rare associations were also observed, including HLA‐A*02:06 with bendamustine and HLA‐Cw alleles with anti‐tuberculosis‐induced DRESS, expanding the spectrum of potential genetic susceptibility [44, 45].

[PMID 42886207] (Pharmacogenomics, 2026) Pharmacogenetics in HIV therapy: a review of key biomarkers, regulatory annotations, and clinical dosing guidelines. Pharmacogenetics is pivotal in modern HIV management, facilitating the transition from the traditional "one-size-fits-all" model toward personalized precision medicine. By analyzing how unique genetic profiles influence pharmacological responses, clinicians can maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing toxicities and adverse drug reactions. Given the high interindividual variability in antiretroviral drug exposure and the necessity for lifelong treatment, identifying key genetic biomarkers is essential to optimize patient safety, treatment adherence, and overall quality of life. This narrative review evaluates major gene-drug associations in HIV therapy, focusing on HLA-B * 57:01 for abacavir, UGT1A1 for atazanavir and dolutegravir, and CYP2B6 for efavirenz. The research includes an exhaustive review of pharmacogenomic databases (e.g. ClinPGx), regulatory agency labels (FDA, EMA, Swissmedic, HC-SC, PMDA), and clinical guidelines from CPIC and DPWG. Integrating pharmacogenetics into clinical practice significantly improves patient safety and treatment adherence. While HLA-B * 57:01 screening is widely implemented, barriers remain for other markers, including logistical challenges and the lack of genomic representation for African and Latin American populations. Clinicians must utilize evidence-based resources and remain updated on this evolving field to effectively tailor antiretroviral regimens and practice precision medicine.

[PMID 41983734] (The Journal of clinical psychiatry, 2026) Proton Pump Inhibitors and the Risk of Dementia. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are the most prescribed gastric acid suppressant drugs; the category includes omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, dexlansoprazole, pantoprazole, and rabeprazole. In 2015, a study suggested that PPI use was associated with an increased risk of dementia. An early meta-analysis confirmed this concern, but the findings were inconsistent in subsequent meta-analyses. Also problematic is that these meta-analyses used questionable approaches, and their findings were characterized by very high heterogeneity. Notably, the high heterogeneity appeared to be driven by large studies with widely different outcomes. Nonetheless, one finding stands out in the body of research examined: older subjects who initiated and continued PPIs (implying chronic use) were at a significantly increased risk of dementia and mild cognitive impairment. Although there are causal and non-causal pathways that associate PPI use with dementia, for reasons that are explained in this article, a cause-effect relationship cannot at present be presumed; so, PPI use is best considered to be a marker of future dementia risk. However, because chronic use of PPIs has been associated with many adverse medical outcomes (eg, disturbances of the gut microbiome, orthopedic complications), and because some PPIs are associated with pharmacokinetic drug interactions (mainly inhibition of CYP2C19), it would be wise to limit the use of PPIs to the shortest duration necessary and to deprescribe PPIs when there does not appear to be need for their continuation.

paragraphs.text: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes are a superfamily of heme-containing enzymes responsible for the phase I metabolism of a wide range of endogenous compounds and xenobiotics, including drugs. CYP enzymes are found predominantly in the liver and small intestine, with lower levels present in the kidneys, lungs, brain, and other tissues. In humans, CYP enzymes are grouped into families and subfamilies based on sequence homology, with CYP1, CYP2, and CYP3 representing the main drug-metabolizing families. The majority of human drug metabolism is mediated by following CYP isoenzymes: CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, and CYP3A4 (Blume et al., 2006). paragraphs.text: In patients with an inadequate response to PPI therapy, CYP2C19 metabolic variability should be considered and therefore dose adjustment, switching to a PPI that is less dependent on CYP2C19 metabolism, or using an alternative acid-suppressive therapy may improve treatment outcomes, particularly in rapid and ultrarapid metabolizers.

As noted in the previous paragraphs, almost all PPIs are metabolized mainly in the liver by CYP enzymes, which may lead to drug to drug interactions. Most cytochrome P450-mediated drug interactions arise from competitive inhibition at the enzyme’s active site, as co-administered substrates compete for the limited metabolic capacity of CYP isoforms (Zanger and Schwab, 2013). Because many commonly prescribed drugs are metabolized by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4, PPIs may increase plasma concentrations of co-administered drugs (Li et al., 2004). In line with this, omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, and dexlansoprazole can affect the activity of these two enzymes, potentially altering the metabolism of other drugs (Stedman and Barclay, 2000; El Rouby et al., 2018; Andersson et al., 2001). [PMID 38163044 | PMC10755811 full text via europepmc_xml] Detection of the T1640C RYR1 mutation indicating malignant hyperthermia in dogs. :: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a pharmacogenetic disorder characterised by a hyper-metabolic response to anaesthetic agents, such as halothane, desflurane, sevoflurane, and isoflurane or the depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine. The clinical symptoms include an unexplained increase in expired carbon dioxide, hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, rhabdomyolysis, acidosis, and hyperkalaemia, as well as cardiac dysrhythmia and renal failure (Roberts et al. 2001; Rosenberg et al. 2015). It was found that the symptoms of MH are a consequence of uncontrolled release of intracellular Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) in skeletal muscles, resulting in their abnormal metabolism (Sambuughin et al. 2005; Jiang et al. 2008). MH occurs not only in humans but also in animals, for example in pigs, but has also been observed in dogs and horses. In dogs (in contrast to humans), in addition to pharmacological triggers it is possible to induce an MH crisis through overexertion and stress (Mealey et al. 2019). The incidence of human MH events during anaesthesia is between 1 : 10 000 and 1 : 250 000 anaesthetics (Halliday 2003) and, on average, patients require three anaesthetics before triggering MH.
Depending on the species, MH is an autosomal dominant or recessive disorder, and so far two genes have been identified whose mutations can be definitely causally linked to MH: RYR1 and CACNA1S. The RYR1 gene codes for the ryanodine receptor, i.e. the Ca2+ channel in the SR membrane. All swine and up to 50% of human MH events appear to be associated with mutations in the RYR1 gene (Roberts et al. 2001). According to Rosenberg et al. (2015), so far 50–70 percent of MH cases associated with more than 400 RYR1 mutations have been identified. Lawal et al. (2020) found that during the last 30 years, 262 publications investigated MH and RYR1-related myopathies in preclinical model systems analysing more than 200 RYR1 variations in a broad range of species including murine, porcine, avian, zebrafish, C. elegans, canine, equine and drosophila. Roberts et al. (2001) established a breeding dog colony through which they proved that MH in dogs is inherited in an autosomal dominant way. Moreover, they revealed that canine MH is caused by the T1640C RYR1 mutation which gives rise to alanine for valine substitution of amino acid 547 (V547A) in the RYR1 protein, and that the MH susceptible (MHS) trait in the pedigree of mixed-breed dogs is in perfect co-segregation with this RYR1 mutation.
Two laboratory in vitro contracture tests are currently used for the diagnosis of MH, which are based on muscle contraction after exposure to halothane or caffeine: the first test (IVCT) was developed by the European Malignant Hyperthermia Group (EMHG), and the second (CHCT) by the North American Malignant Hyperthermia Group (NAMHG) (The European Malignant Hyperpyrexia Group 1984; Larach et al. 1992). [PMID 42524381 | PMC13411286 full text via pmc_xml] Investigation of the Prevalence of the HLA-B*15:02 Allele in the Asian Populations: A Comprehensive Analysis Through Using AFND. :: A set of cell surface proteins called the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) has a vital role in the activation of T‐cells, as the activation process necessitates the complementary engagement of T‐cell receptors with the antigenic peptides bound to the MHC molecules. The human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the MHC present in humans, which is encoded by the HLA gene complex, situated on chromosome 6's short arm. Based on the locus and function of the coding gene, biochemistry, and tissue distribution, the HLA antigens are grouped under two clusters (i.e., class I and II). Three loci (i.e., classical HLA‐A, HLA‐B, and HLA‐C genes) encode for the molecules of HLA class‐I [1, 2]. The HLA genes exhibit a great degree of polymorphism resulting from different mutations, gene conversion, and meiotic recombination, accounting for a huge variability in the expression of HLA molecules [1, 2, 3, 4]. At present, more than 28,000 HLA class‐I alleles have been identified [5].
From a pharmacogenomics (PGx) perspective, HLA interactions have been associated with adverse drug reactions, resulting in hospitalization and even mortality, due to the drug‐induced hypersensitivity reactions (HSR) for several clinically important drugs. Due to the co‐dominant expression of HLA, the absence or presence of certain related HLA alleles dictates the susceptibility of drug‐induced HSR [1, 6, 7]. HLA‐B*15:02 is one such important allele that has been associated with the severe cutaneous adverse drug reactions (SCARs) of multiple extensively used drugs (e.g., carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, etc.) [8, 9, 10, 11]. However, the allele frequency of specific HLA alleles has been reported to exhibit significant variability across different ethnicities and populations [2]. Safe prescribing and effective medication review during acute hospitalization depends on accurate information about liver and kidney function because these organs are responsible for the elimination of most medications. While estimates for kidney function are widely used, comparable markers of hepatic drug-metabolizing capacity are not routinely available. We evaluated the clinical relevance of pharmacogenomic (PGx) information for key pharmacogenes implicated in medication elimination in older adults presenting to the emergency department. Fourteen pharmacogenes were analysed using the Personal Medicine Profile™ test. GeneYouIn PillCheck™ software performed genotype-to-phenotype translations, identified drug-gene interactions (DGIs) and generated a clinical decision report based on each patient's actual medication use. Among 125 acutely admitted older medical patients (median age 78.3 years; 10 medications; 7 chronic diseases), PGx testing identified 88 DGIs across 63 patients (50.4%). Of these, 46.5% were considered by clinical experts to be clinically relevant for the individual patient, affecting 33 patients (26.4%) in the total study population. [PMID 41860236 | PMC13140828 full text via pmc_xml] Impact of Pharmacokinetic Gene Polymorphisms on Statin-Induced Myotoxicity in Thai Patients Treated With Simvastatin. :: Statins are effective for reducing low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C), yet many patients fail to achieve target lipid levels due to adverse effects, leading to discontinuation rates between 8.2% and 54% that are associated with increased LDL‐C levels and a higher risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and mortality [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. In the Thai healthcare setting, simvastatin is a cornerstone of lipid‐lowering therapy as a fully reimbursed agent listed in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) [8]. Its extensive usage is further supported by the 2025 Clinical Practice Guidelines by the Royal College of Physicians of Thailand (RCPT), which recommend starting moderate‐intensity statins, such as simvastatin, for primary prevention in high‐risk populations, while reserving restricted high‐intensity options for second‐line intensification [9]. Given its predominant use, simvastatin was selected as the focus of this study to reflect real‐world prescribing patterns and patient exposure in Thailand. However, myotoxicity is the most common adverse effect of statin therapy. The clinical spectrum of statin‐induced myotoxicity (SIM) varies widely, from mild, asymptomatic creatine kinase (CK) elevation, myopathy, myalgia, and myositis, to severe, life‐threatening rhabdomyolysis. Such muscle symptoms can affect 70%–80% of patients, disrupting daily activities, and in rare cases, severe rhabdomyolysis requires hospitalization [10, 11].
SIM is a dose‐dependent adverse effect, with higher systemic exposure increasing the risk [12]. This underscores the critical role of pharmacokinetic factors in the development of SIM. The systemic exposure to simvastatin is influenced by polymorphisms in several genes encoding drug‐metabolizing enzymes and transporters, including CYP3A4/5 (cytochrome P450 3A4/5), ABCB1 (P‐glycoprotein), ABCC2 (ATP‐binding cassette subfamily C member 2), ABCG2 (ATP‐binding cassette subfamily G member 2), and SLCO1B1/1B3 (organic anion‐transporting polypeptides 1B1/1B3) [13]. Among these, the SLCO1B1 gene, which plays a pivotal role in hepatic statin uptake, has been strongly associated with SIM risk [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. Specifically, the SLCO1B1*5 (c.521T>C, rs4149056) and SLCO1B1*15 (c.521T>C and c.388A>G, rs2306283) alleles are known to impair OATP1B1 transporter function [20], reducing hepatic drug clearance and increasing systemic statin levels. This pharmacogenetic variation results in increased SIM risk [21].

[PMID 42907239] (Pediatrics and neonatology, 2026) The prevalence and impacts of NUDT15 variants in pediatric-onset inflammatory bowel disease patients in Taiwan. Thiopurines are important therapeutic agents for patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and the Nudix hydrolase 15 (NUDT15) gene has been reported to be associated with the safety of thiopurine use. We investigated the prevalence of NUDT15 variants and their impacts in the pediatric-onset IBD group in Taiwan. Seventy-three pediatric-onset IBD patients followed up at National Taiwan University Hospital from 2023 to 2025 were recruited. Every patient had NUDT15 genotyping and was classified as one of three phenotypes: the normal, intermediate, and poor metabolizers. The association of NUDT15 genotypes, phenotypes, thiopurine dosage, and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) was analyzed. According to NUDT15 genotypes, 58 patients (79.45%) were normal metabolizers, 12 (16.44%) were intermediate metabolizers, and 3 (4.11%) were poor metabolizers in this cohort. Neutropenia occurred in 9 of 48 patients (18.75%) who had thiopurine use. Three thiopurine users (6.25%) developed severe neutropenia, including two poor metabolizers. The intermediate and poor metabolizers are significantly associated with neutropenia in thiopurine users (OR = 13.39, 95% CI = 2.50-71.64, p = 0.002). The mutant allele NUDT15*3 and NUDT15*6 had a higher frequency in our cohort than the East Asian group. The NUDT15 variants are significantly associated with neutropenia in thiopurine users. The prevalence of poor metabolizers is higher in our study group compared to other East Asian areas, and the distribution of NUDT15 genotypes is different. Preemptive NUDT15 genotyping, including NUDT15*3 and NUDT15*6, should be considered in the pediatric-onset IBD group.

paragraphs.text: Thiopurines are important therapeutic agents for patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and the Nudix hydrolase 15 (NUDT15) gene has been reported to be associated with the safety of thiopurine use. We investigated the prevalence of NUDT15 variants and their impacts in the pediatric-onset IBD group in Taiwan. Seventy-three pediatric-onset IBD patients followed up at National Taiwan University Hospital from 2023 to 2025 were recruited. Every patient had NUDT15 genotyping and was classified as one of three phenotypes: the normal, intermediate, and poor metabolizers. The association of NUDT15 genotypes, phenotypes, thiopurine dosage, and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) was analyzed. paper_digests.summary: The paper discusses the association between NUDT15 variants and thiopurine-induced neutropenia in pediatric-onset IBD patients. It highlights that intermediate and poor metabolizers are significantly associated with neutropenia, suggesting a need for preemptive genotyping of NUDT15 before initiating thiopurine therapy.

paragraphs.text: This study provides a clinically prioritized pharmacogenomic frequency resource for Kazakh, Russian, and Uzbek population groups residing in Kazakhstan. A total of 112 directly genotyped ClinPGx-selected variants with evidence levels 1A, 1B, and 2A were analyzed for population-specific allele and genotype frequencies. Several clinically relevant variants showed marked differences between the study groups, including NUDT15 rs116855232, SLCO1B1 rs4149056, VKORC1 rs9934438, and UGT1A1 rs10929302, whereas CYP4F2 rs2108622 and CYP2B6 rs3745274 were observed at broadly comparable frequencies across the three groups.

[PMID 42898061] (Pulmonology, 2026) Non-eligibility for highly effective modulator therapy with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in cystic fibrosis: What about Portugal? Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene. CFTR modulators are drugs developed to target the defective protein. All over the world, there are patients considered non-eligible for this therapy according to local regulatory policies. To characterise the Portuguese CF patients defined as non-eligible according to genotype for highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT) with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), the authors conducted a multicentre observational study based on a retrospective analysis of the Portuguese CF population. Based on the current prescribing policy in Portugal, the prevalence of non-eligible patients in Portugal in 2023 was 18.7%, similar to that reported in Europe. However, the regulatory acceleration in the CFTR modulator landscape in 2025 will most likely decrease the expected prevalence to 1.2% under national regulatory adoption of EMA criteria. R334W, G85E, N1303K, G542X, A561E, R1066C and P205S are the most prevalent variants. Most patients are young adults with established pulmonary disease. CF therapies impose a considerable burden on this population. This study provides a deeper understanding of the Portuguese CF population currently ineligible for ETI and enables the projection of the potential impact that forthcoming changes in HEMT eligibility criteria may have across Portugal. With the anticipated expansion of these criteria, the number of patients remaining ineligible for HEMT is expected to become residual. Furthermore, the present work offers a characterisation of patients likely to remain ineligible for HEMT in the future, who could be suitable candidates for clinical trials exploring alternative therapeutic approaches.

paper_digests.title: CFTR Functional Rescue and Heterogeneous Clinical Outcomes Following Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor Therapy in People with Cystic Fibrosis Carrying the W1282R Variant.

paragraphs.text: W1282R is currently included among CFTR variants associated with eligibility for ETI therapy. According to the TRIKAFTA prescribing information, W1282R is listed as responsive to ETI based on in vitro data from the Fisher rat thyroid (FRT) cell assay [14]. However, clinical data on ETI therapy in people carrying W1282R, and particularly data linking ex vivo functional responses with clinical outcomes, remain very limited. To our knowledge, no previous study has combined longitudinal clinical outcomes during ETI therapy in people with CF carrying W1282R with functional data obtained from patient-derived biological material.

paragraphs.section: 2.3. Functional Assessment of Response to ETI
paragraphs.text: In the absence of CFTR modulators, W1282R organoids showed very low residual CFTR activity. Following stimulation with 5 μM forskolin, W1282R/394delTT (P8) organoids exhibited minimal swelling, similar to that observed in F508del/F508del organoids, whereas W1282R/CFTRdele2,3 (P4) organoids showed virtually no response to forskolin stimulation (Figure 5 and Figure 6).

paragraphs.section: 2.3. Functional Assessment of Response to ETI
paragraphs.text: Incubation with CFTR modulator combinations resulted in forskolin-induced organoid swelling, indicating increased CFTR-mediated fluid transport. The greatest FIS response was observed with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor. Compared with forskolin alone, ETI significantly increased FIS in both W1282R organoid cultures (p < 0.001 for each culture). In both W1282R organoid cultures, area under the curve (AUC) values reached approximately 3000 arbitrary units (a.u.), whereas the response in the F508del/F508del reference culture was greater, with an AUC of approximately 4700 a.u.

Tissue-dependent differences in response to CFTR modulators have also been described for the N1303K variant. According to Pranke et al., ETI therapy was associated with restoration of CFTR function in functional assays, while sweat test values remained abnormal in some patients. The authors interpreted this as a manifestation of tissue-specific and incomplete restoration of N1303K-CFTR function [7]. Our findings suggest that a similar response pattern may also occur in patients carrying the W1282R variant.

[PMID 42614302 | PMC13481457 full text via europepmc_xml] Identification of a large DPYD gene deletion undetected by standard genotyping in a patient with severe capecitabine-related toxicity: a case report. :: Fluoropyrimidines, including 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) and the oral prodrug capecitabine, are widely used both as single agents and as part of combination regimens in various solid tumors, such as gastrointestinal, breast and head/neck cancers (Longley et al., 2003).
Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD), encoded by the DPYD gene, is a key enzyme involved in the metabolism of 5-FU and its prodrugs, converting more than 80% of 5-FU into inactive metabolites (Diasio and Harris, 1989). DPD deficiency, which affects about the 3%–7% of Caucasian population, leads to excessive concentrations of the active metabolites of 5-FU and consequent severe toxicity (myelosuppression, diarrhea, mucositis, neurotoxicity), which is fatal in approximately 1% of patients (Knikman et al., 2021).
Various genotyping or phenotyping approaches have been developed to assess DPD deficiency and are routinely used in clinical practice to individualize dosing of fluoropyrimidines and reduce the incidence of severe toxicity (Henricks et al., 2018a; Bignucolo et al., 2023), particularly grade 4–5 events, which DPYD pathogenic variants strongly predict (Le Teuff et al., 2024).
The European Medicines Agency (EMA) recommends two methods for DPD deficiency testing before starting cancer treatment including fluoropyrimidine: phenotyping by measuring pre-treatment plasmatic uracil concentration or genotyping for the presence of DPYD risk variant alleles, namely c.1905 + 1G>A (rs3918290), c.1679T>G (rs55886062), c.2846A>T (rs67376798), c.1129-5923C>G (rs75017182) (European Medicines Agency, 2020). Although phenotyping appears to be a more comprehensive approach to identify patients with impaired enzymatic activity as compared to genotyping (Etienne-Grimaldi et al., 2023), it is currently challenged by several pre-analytical issues, which make a wide routine application difficult (Knikman et al., 2025). On the other hand, genotyping of a limited panel, as proposed by current pharmacogenetic guidelines, limits the efficiency in identifying all the patients at risk of severe toxicity. Population-specific or rare DPYD variants, which are not always detected by standard genotyping testing, can lead to severe and potentially life-threatening toxicity from fluoropyrimidines (De Mattia et al., 2022; De Mattia et al., 2025; De Mattia et al., 2024). New sequencing technologies, such as NGS, may contribute to capture rare genetic alterations (Larrue et al., 2024).
In this report, we present the case of a patient with gastric adenocarcinoma, wild-type for the 4 most common DPYD variants, treated with full-dose capecitabine-based chemotherapy in the adjuvant setting, who experienced severe fluoropyrimidine-related toxicity due to a large heterozygous deletion in DPYD.

Tumor organoids and pharmacogenetic profiling represent two rapidly advancing tools in precision oncology. Organoids provide physiologically relevant three-dimensional models that retain the genomic, architectural and functional features of patient tumors, enabling high-fidelity drug testing. In parallel, germline pharmacogenetic variation significantly influences chemotherapy metabolism, efficacy and toxicity, particularly in breast cancer. Integrating these approaches offers a powerful framework for individualized therapy selection. A narrative review methodology was used to synthesize recent evidence (2006-2025) from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and ScienceDirect. Eligible studies included original research on tumor organoid engineering, microenvironmental modelling, drug-response profiling, vascular and immune co-culture systems, and pharmacogenetic determinants of chemotherapy response. Findings were organized thematically across domains of organoid fidelity, microenvironment reconstruction, drug-response prediction, and clinically relevant pharmacogenetic variants. Organoid studies demonstrated high establishment rates, preservation of tumor heterogeneity and improved modeling of stromal, vascular and immune components. paper_digests.title: Identification of a large DPYD gene deletion undetected by standard genotyping in a patient with severe capecitabine-related toxicity: a case report.

paragraphs.text: The SNP array detected a 545.3 Kb deletion at chromosome 1p21.3 from the distal SNP at base pair 97176283 to the proximal SNP at base pair 97721542 [GRCh38] (Figure 2). The deletion includes 494 clones with an average Log R value of −0.481.This region encompasses DPYD gene associated with _Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency _(#274270_; _AR_) _and_ 5-fluorouracil toxicity _(#274270; AR). The entire gene DPYD is covered by 770 SNP clones and the deletion is completely within the gene, from exon 5 to exon 20.

In this study we identified a large heterozygous deletion spanning from exon 5 to exon 20 of DPYD gene that was found to be associated with a strong decrease in the enzyme activity and likely to be related to the observed toxic event. In our case report the phenotypic effect of the observed genomic alteration was evaluated by assessing enzymatic activity in PBMCs which was found to be reduced by 49% as compared to two wild type healthy donors. This finding was further supported by the analysis of plasma U and DHU. Based on published data, a plasma uracil threshold of 16 ng/mL was used to discriminate between normal and deficient DPD activity, with DPD deficiency defined by U concentrations >16 ng/mL (Knikman et al., 2021; Contu et al., 2025). The DHU/U ratio was also considered to support

It has been previously documented that DPYD deletions account for approximately 7% of DPD deficiency cases (van Kuilenburg et al., 2009). Several cases have been described in which severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity was observed despite routine DPYD genotyping being negative and subsequently associated with rare intragenic deletions or other structural variants detectable only through extensive genomic analysis (van Kuilenburg et al., 2010; Wigle et al., 2023; Malekkou et al., 2024; Saarenheimo et al., 2021). In several cases, profound mucosal toxicity has been reported to precede systemic complications, including sepsis (García-González et al., 2018; de Haar-Holleman et al., 2024; Ly et al., 2020; Tong et al., 2018; Henricks et al., 2018b).

In this case report a case of severe capecitabine-related toxicity in a patient with a large DPYD deletion not detected by routine pre-treatment panel genotyping was described. This case highlights the limitations of current pharmacogenetic screening for the initiation of a fluoropyrimidine-based therapy and emphasizes the importance of integrating genomic and functional strategies in selected cases. Current national guideline recommendations (AIOM-SIF Working Group, 2024), based on DPYD variants most strongly associated with reduced enzyme function, have improved the safety of fluoropyrimidine use, thanks to studies on variant-associated toxicity, most notably the meta-analysis by Meulendijks et al. generated_answer: The study indicates a significant relationship between low plasma vitamin K concentrations and warfarin sensitivity, suggesting that VKORC1 genotype influences warfarin dose requirements. However, the evidence for this association remains conflicting, with ClinPGx curators recording inconsistent reports regarding VKORC1's impact on warfarin therapy outcomes. The biological mechanism involves substrate-limited conditions where low vitamin K levels exacerbate warfarin-induced inhibition of GGCX-mediated γ-carboxylation, leading to higher PT-INR values at given warfarin concentrations. For drug development and patient safety, it is crucial to validate the clinical relevance of plasma PK concentration thresholds during warfarin therapy and consider dietary VK intake in dose adjustment strategies. CPIC guidelines for phenprocoumon are based on VKORC1 genetic variants, indicating a need for similar evaluations for other vitamin K antagonists like warfarin.

The study aimed to investigate the relationship between plasma vitamin K (VK) concentrations and warfarin sensitivity, focusing on phylloquinone (PK) and menaquinone-4 (MK4). The BASE model included established clinical and genetic factors affecting warfarin dose requirements. Incorporating an indicator of low PK concentration (<0.20 ng/mL) improved the prediction of Warfarin Sensitivity Index (WSI), while continuous or spline models for PK and MK4 showed limited improvement. This suggests that the impact of plasma VK concentrations on warfarin sensitivity is more pronounced at lower levels rather than across a broad range.

1. **Baseline Model**: The BASE model included factors such as S-warfarin concentration, R-warfarin concentration, age, height, sex, renal function, VKORC1 genotype (rs9923231), CYP4F2 genotype (rs2108622), CYP2C9 genotype, and CYP2C19 genotype. This model served as the foundation for evaluating additional factors.

2. **Impact of Low PK Concentration**: The addition of an indicator for low plasma PK concentration (<0.20 ng/mL) to the BASE model significantly improved WSI prediction (ΔR² = 0.384). This indicates that patients with lower PK levels exhibit higher warfarin sensitivity, which is consistent with previous studies showing that dietary VK intake influences warfarin dose requirements.

3. **Genetic and Clinical Factors**: The multivariable linear regression analysis showed that plasma PK concentration <0.20 ng/mL was independently associated with higher WSI after adjusting for established clinical and genetic factors (p-value = 0.033). This suggests that low PK levels are a significant predictor of warfarin sensitivity beyond the influence of other known variables.

4. **Mechanistic Insights**: The study proposes that at lower VK concentrations, changes in VK availability may have a more substantial impact on GGCX-mediated γ-carboxylation due to substrate-limited conditions. Warfarin inhibition further reduces the reduced VK cofactor required for GGCX, leading to less efficient carboxylation of VK-dependent coagulation factors and higher PT-INR at given warfarin concentrations.

5. **Comparison with MK4**: While both PK and MK4 can serve as cofactors for GGCX in vitro, their effects on coagulation and tissue disposition may differ. The study observed a clearer association between WSI and low plasma PK concentration compared to MK4, suggesting that PK more directly reflects exogenous VK supply.

6. **Limitations**: The study included patients already receiving stable warfarin therapy, limiting the ability to assess pretreatment PT-INR values accurately. Additionally, the small number of patients with low plasma PK concentrations and limited genotype subgroup sizes reduced statistical power for evaluating interactions between genetic or clinical variables and low plasma VK status.

7. **Future Directions**: Future studies should validate the clinically relevant range of plasma PK concentrations during warfarin therapy, including the exploratory <0.20 ng/mL threshold identified in this study. Additionally, larger cohorts with prespecified interaction hypotheses are needed to formally assess potential effect modification and establish strategies for managing patients with markedly low plasma VK levels.

[PMID 42823629] (Basic & clinical pharmacology & toxicology, 2026) Limitations of VKORC1 rs9934438 as a Surrogate Marker for Vitamin K Antagonist Dose Adjustment. VKORC1 genetic variants are major determinants of interindividual variability in vitamin K antagonist (VKA) dose requirements and are incorporated into several pharmacogenetic dosing guidelines. The promoter variant rs9923231 is considered the clinically relevant marker for genotype-guided VKA dosing. However, the intronic variant rs9934438 is sometimes used as a surrogate marker because it is assumed to be in strong linkage disequilibrium with rs9923231. We aimed to assess whether rs9934438 can reliably substitute rs9923231 in clinical practice. We conducted a retrospective, single-centre study including 939 patients who underwent pharmacogenetic testing. Both variants were genotyped using a TaqMan OpenArray custom panel. Concordance between rs9934438 and rs9923231 was evaluated, and the diagnostic performance of rs9934438 for predicting clinically relevant rs9923231 diplotypes was assessed. Although concordance was high overall, rs9934438 misclassified two patients who, according to rs9923231, required a reduced VKA dose, resulting in potential false-negative classifications. These findings indicate that, while rs9934438 provides informative results in most cases, it may fail to identify some patients requiring dose adjustment. Our results highlight the clinical implications of relying on surrogate markers in pharmacogenetic-guided VKA therapy and support the preferential use of rs9923231 to ensure accurate individualized dosing and optimize treatment safety.

Warfarin sensitivity exhibits marked interindividual variability, partly explained by genetic polymor -
phisms affecting vitamin K (VK) metabolism. However, the association between plasma VK concentrations 
and warfarin sensitivity remains unclear. We investigated this association in Japanese patients receiving 
warfarin therapy. Blood samples from patients aged ≥20 years were analyzed for genetic polymorphisms 
associated with warfarin sensitivity, warfarin concentrations, and plasma concentrations of phylloquinone 
(PK) and menaquinone-4 (MK4). The warfarin sensitivity index (WSI) was calculated as the change in pro -
thrombin time-international normalized ratio per S-warfarin-equivalent concentration. Among 105 patients, 
plasma PK and MK4 concentrations were not significantly correlated with WSI when analyzed as continuous 
variables ( p = 0.297 and p = 0.118, respectively). To determine whether plasma VK concentrations provided 
additional predictive information, WSI prediction models with and without VK variables were compared. 
Incorporating an indicator of plasma PK concentration <0.20 ng/mL improved model performance, whereas 
MK4-based models showed no clear improvement. In multivariable analysis, a plasma PK concentration 
<0.20 ng/mL was independently associated with a higher WSI after adjustment for established clinical and 
genetic factors (B = 0.703, 95% confidence interval, 0.057–1.349; p = 0.033). These findings suggest that a low 
plasma PK concentration may explain some of the interindividual variability in warfarin sensitivity beyond 
that accounted for by genetic polymorphisms. Direct measurement of plasma PK may provide additional 
information for understanding increased warfarin sensitivity in patients with low VK status.

However, these genetic and other known factors collectively 
explain only approximately 50% of the interindividual vari -

pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic factors may contrib -

Reduced VK serves as an essential cofactor for GGCX-  
mediated γ-glutamyl carboxylation, a post-translational modi -
fication required for the functional activation of VK-dependent 
coagulation factors. 4–7) VK occurs in several forms, including 
phylloquinone (PK; vitamin K1), which is obtained mainly 
from green leafy vegetables, and menaquinone-4 (MK4), 
a vitamin K2 homologue found mainly in animal-derived 
foods.6,24) Although VK supplementation has been associated 
with warfarin efficacy and prothrombin time-international 
normalized ratio (PT-INR) variability, 24–36) the concentration–
response relationship between plasma VK concentrations and 
warfarin efficacy in humans remains unexplored. Furthermore, 
the extent to which VKORC1 and CYP4F2 polymorphisms 
influence VK pharmacokinetics is not fully understood. 
Therefore, relying solely on genetic polymorphism analysis 
may be insufficient to assess the contribution of VK pharma -
cokinetics to interindividual variability in warfarin efficacy.
To better understand individual differences in warfarin 
efficacy beyond those explained by plasma warfarin concen -
trations, evaluating VK status may provide additional insight. 
Accordingly, we conducted an integrated analysis of plasma 
VK concentrations together with genetic and nongenetic fac -
tors influencing warfarin sensitivity. The primary aim of this 
study was to investigate the association between plasma VK 
concentrations and warfarin sensitivity.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Study Population This study included Japanese patients aged 
≥20 years who were receiving warfarin therapy at the Department 
of Cardiology, Gunma University Hospital, or the Department of 
Internal Medicine, Japan Community Health Care Organization 
(JCHO) Gunma Chuo Hospital. Patients without PT-INR mea -
surements and those with cirrhosis or liver cancer were excluded. 
Whole blood samples were used for genetic polymorphism anal-
ysis, and plasma samples were used to determine the S-warfarin, 
R-warfarin, PK, and MK4 concentrations. Patient demographics, 
warfarin dosages, and laboratory data were obtained from elec -
tronic medical records. The study population overlapped with that 
of a previous study,23) except for three patients who were excluded 
because of insufficient plasma samples for warfarin and VK 
analyses. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Com -
mittee of Takasaki University of Health and Welfare (approval no. 
2338), the Ethics Committee of Gunma University (approval no. 
HS2020-170), and the Ethics Committee of JCHO Gunma Chuo 
Hospital (approval no. 2022-009), and the study was conducted 
in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed 
consent was obtained from all patients.
Genotype Detection  Genomic DNA was extracted from 
whole blood using the QIAamp ® Blood Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, 
CA, U.S.A.). Seven single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) 
were analyzed using TaqMan genotyping assays (Applied 
Biosystems, Foster City, CA, U.S.A.): VKORC1 rs9923231, 
CYP2C9*3 (rs1057910), CYP4F2*3 (rs2108622), CYP2C19*2 
(rs4244285), CYP2C19*3 (rs4986893), GGCX rs699664, and 
GGCX rs12714145. TaqMan primer and probe sets for each 
SNP allele were included in the kits. The specific assays 
used were as follows: VKORC1 rs9923231, C__30403261_20; 
CYP2C9*3 rs1057910, C_ _27104892_10; CYP4F2*3 rs2108622, 
C__16179493_40; CYP2C19*2 rs4244285, C__25986767_70; 
CYP2C19*3 rs4986893, C__27861809_10; GGCX rs699664, 
C_ _1036123_10; and GGCX rs12714145, C_ _31839079_10. 
TaqMan assays were performed using an Mx3000P instrument 
(Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, U.S.A.) according to 
the PCR cycling conditions recommended by Applied Biosys -
tems. CYP2C19 metabolizer status was categorized as rapid 
metabolizer (*1/*1), intermediate metabolizer (*1/*2 or *1/*3), 
or poor metabolizer (*2/*2, *2/*3, or *3/*3).
Sample Preparation of Warfarin and VK Sample pre -
treatment for warfarin quantification was performed according 
to the method described by Putriana et al .37) Briefly, 100 µL 
of plasma was mixed with 10 µL of a 0.5 -µg/mL griseofulvin 
solution as the internal standard, followed by the addition 
of 500 µL of acetonitrile. After vortex mixing, the sample 
was centrifuged at 13000 rpm for 4 min at 4°C. The resulting 
supernatant was evaporated to dryness under reduced pres -
sure, and the residue was reconstituted in 100 µL of the mobile 
phase before HPLC with fluorescence detection (HPLC-FLR) 
analysis.
Sample pretreatment for VK quantification was performed 
according to the method described by Ohno et al .,38) with 
PK-13C6 and MK4- 13C6 used as internal standards for PK and 
MK4, respectively. Briefly, 50 µL of an internal standard solution 
containing PK-13C6 and MK4- 13C6 at 5 ng/mL each was added 
to 0.4 mL of plasma, followed by the addition of 2 mL of etha -
nol. After vortex mixing for 1 min, 6 mL of hexane was added. 
The sample was vigorously shaken for 5 min and centrifuged at 
3000 rpm for 10 min. The upper hexane layer was collected and 
evaporated to dryness under reduced pressure. The residue was 
reconstituted in 100 µL of methanol before ultra-performance 
LC–MS analysis. All sample preparation procedures were per -
formed under protection from light.
HPLC with Fluorescence Detection Conditions for 
Warfarin S-warfarin and R-warfarin concentrations were 
determined using HPLC-FLR. LC and fluorescence detec -
tion were performed using an LC-20AD system (Shimadzu 
Corporation, Kyoto, Japan) and an RF-20A XS fluorescence 
detector (Shimadzu Corporation), respectively. Separation was 
achieved using a Chiralcel OD-RH column (4.6 × 150 mm; 
Daicel Chemical Industries, Tokyo, Japan). The LC conditions 
were as follows: column temperature, 40°C; mobile phase, an 
isocratic mixture of 65% 2 mM phosphate buffer (pH 2.0) and 
35% acetonitrile; flow rate, 0.5 mL/min; and injection volume, 
25 µL. Fluorescence detection was performed at excitation 
and emission wavelengths of 310 and 350 nm, respectively, for 
warfarin and 310 and 400 nm, respectively, for griseofulvin.
Ultra-Performance LC–MS Conditions for VK Atmo-
spheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI) mass spectrometry

The LC conditions were as follows: column temperature, 40°C; 
mobile phases, 0.1% formic acid in Milli-Q water (A) and meth-
anol (B); flow rate, 0.3 mL/min; gradient program, 90–98% B in 
3 min, 98% B in 15 min, and 98–90% B in 0.5 min; and injec -
tion volume, 10 µL. Mass spectrometric analysis was performed 
using a 3200 QTRAP mass spectrometer (AB Sciex) with APCI 
in positive-ion mode. The ionization parameters were as fol -
lows: capillary voltage, 1000 V; desolvation temperature, 500°C; 
source temperature, 150°C; desolvation gas flow, 1000 L/h; and 
cone gas flow, 70 L/h. The transitions m/z 451.3 > 187.2 for PK, 
m/z 445.2 > 187.3 for MK4, m/z 457.3 > 193.1 for PK-13C6, and 
m/z 451.3 > 193.1 for MK4-13C6 were monitored. The decluster -
ing potential, entrance potential, and collision energy were 56, 
5.0, and 33 V, respectively, for PK; 41, 4.0, and 31 V, respec-
tively, for MK4; 56, 6.5, and 31 V, respectively, for PK-13C6; and 
41, 6.0, and 33 V, respectively, for MK4-13C6.

Prediction Modeling and Correction–Effect Analy -
sis For WSI-based prediction modeling, the VK-free base 
model included age, height, sex, renal function, VKORC1 
rs9923231, CYP4F2*3 rs2108622, and comorbid cancer. Addi -
tional models were constructed by adding plasma PK con -
centration, plasma MK4 concentration, indicators of low VK 
concentrations, or spline terms for plasma PK and MK4 con -
centrations to the VK-free base model, and their performance 
was compared with that of the base model.
To evaluate the VK-related correction effect on WSI pre -
diction, the WSI predicted by the VK-free base model was 
subtracted from that predicted by each VK-added model. This 
difference was defined as the VK-related correction effect. 
To determine whether the findings of the WSI-based analysis 
were also reflected in the clinically observed anticoagulant 
response, an additional analysis was performed using PT-INR 
as the outcome. In this model, S-warfarin and R-warfarin 
concentrations were included as explanatory variables, with 
adjustment for age, height, sex, renal function, VKORC1, 
CYP4F2, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19 genotypes, and comorbid 
cancer. The change in model performance after the addition 
of VK variables was then evaluated. PK or MK4 concentra -
tions recorded as 0 because they were below the lower limit of 
quantification were replaced with one-half of the correspond -
ing lower limit of quantification before analysis.
Statistical Analyses For analyses of the associations of 
clinical and genetic factors with WSI, correlations between 
continuous variables and WSI were assessed using Pearson’s 
correlation analysis, whereas WSI values were compared 
between two groups using the Mann–Whitney U test. Genetic 
polymorphisms were categorized into two groups based on 
ANOVA with post hoc  analysis: strongly associated geno -
types and other genotypes. Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium was 
assessed using Pearson’s goodness-of-fit χ2 test. The associa -
tions of plasma PK and MK4 concentrations with WSI were 
assessed using Pearson’s correlation analysis. Plasma PK and 
MK4 concentrations were compared between genotype groups 
of CYP4F2*3 rs2108622 and VKORC1 rs9923231 using the 
Mann–Whitney U test. Prediction models were constructed 
using multivariable linear regression analysis. The VK-added 
models included PK or MK4 as continuous variables, an indi -
cator of low PK concentration, or spline terms. For the spline 
models, plasma PK and MK4 concentrations were natural-log 
transformed, and the models were fitted using B-spline basis 
functions with 4 degrees of freedom. Model performance 
was assessed using five-fold cross-validation, with R 2, mean 
absolute error (MAE), and root mean squared error (RMSE) 
calculated from the pooled out-of-fold predictions. Finally, 
multivariable linear regression analysis was performed to 
identify factors independently associated with WSI. The pri -
mary model included a binary indicator of low plasma PK 
concentration (PK <0.20 ng/mL), VKORC1 rs9923231, and 
variables associated with WSI in the univariate analysis (age, 
height, sex, estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR], and 
CYP4F2*3 rs2108622). Comorbid cancer was not included in 
the final model because only three patients had comorbid can -
cer. As a sensitivity analysis, multivariable linear regression 
analysis was repeated using the same explanatory variables 
after excluding these three patients. An additional model was 
constructed in which plasma PK and MK4 concentrations 
were simultaneously entered as continuous variables. All sta -
tistical analyses were performed using SPSS software, version 
26.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, U.S.A.), and exploratory spline-
based analyses were performed using Python (Python Soft -
ware Foundation, Wilmington, DE, U.S.A.). A p-value <0.05 
was considered statistically significant.

patients receiving warfarin therapy are summarized in Table 
1. The coefficients of variation for plasma PK and MK4 con -
centrations were 72.8 and 86.2%, respectively. Atrial fibril -
lation was the most common indication for warfarin therapy.

Factors Associated with Individual Differences in 
WSI The results of the multivariable linear regression anal -
ysis are presented in Table 6 . The model included plasma 
PK concentration dichotomized at 0.20 ng/mL, VKORC1 
rs9923231, and variables associated with WSI in the univariable 
analyses: age, height, sex, eGFR, and CYP4F2*3 rs2108622. 
MK4 was not included in the final model because the 
spline-based correction curve did not show a clear threshold-  
like pattern. No multicollinearity was detected between 
plasma PK concentration and the other variables. In the 
multivariable analysis, low plasma PK concentration, eGFR 
<30 mL/min/1.73 m2, and VKORC1 rs9923231 genotype were 
independently associated with higher WSI. Specifically, 
plasma PK concentration <0.20 ng/mL was independently 
associated with higher WSI (B = 0.703, 95% confidence inter -
val [CI], 0.057 to 1.349; p = 0.033). In the sensitivity analysis 
excluding the three patients with comorbid cancer, plasma PK 
concentration <0.20 ng/mL remained independently associated 
with higher WSI (B = 0.799, 95% CI, 0.179 to 1.419; p = 0.012; 
Supplementary Table S1). When plasma PK and MK4 concen -
trations were included as continuous variables, neither was 
significantly associated with WSI (Supplementary Table S2).
DISCUSSION
In this study, we investigated the association between 
plasma VK concentrations and warfarin sensitivity, which 
remains poorly understood. Although plasma PK and MK4 
concentrations showed negative correlations with WSI, these 
associations were not statistically significant when the con -
centrations were analyzed as continuous variables. However,

prediction modeling showed that incorporating an indicator 
of low plasma PK concentration, defined as PK <0.20 ng/mL, 
improved WSI prediction compared with the VK-free base 
model. In contrast, models incorporating PK as a continu -
ous variable or spline term and MK4-based models showed 
limited or no improvement. Visualization of the VK-related 
correction effects showed that the contribution of PK was most 
pronounced at low plasma concentrations and approached zero 
at approximately 0.20 ng/mL. An additional analysis using 
PT-INR as the outcome showed a similar pattern. Further -
more, multivariable linear regression analysis demonstrated 
that plasma PK concentration <0.20 ng/mL was independently 
associated with higher WSI after adjustment for established 
clinical and genetic factors. Collectively, these findings sug -
gest that the association between plasma PK concentration and 
warfarin sensitivity may be more apparent at low PK concen -
trations than across the entire concentration range.
Plant-derived PK, as a component of dietary VK, can influ -
ence warfarin sensitivity. 16,21,24–36) Specifically, in warfarin-  
treated patients with stable PT-INR, daily PK intakes of 
150 µg for women and 200 µg for men have been reported to 
significantly reduce mean INR. 27) Other studies have reported 
that a PK intake of 100–200 µg/d may help maintain PT-INR 
within the therapeutic range. 16,27,29,31–35) Conversely, Tanaka  
et al .21) demonstrated that VK intake independently contrib -
uted to the warfarin maintenance dose, although its effect was 
small. They suggested that factors such as VK synthesis by 
the gut microbiota and variability in VK metabolism associ -
ated with CYP4F2 genetic polymorphisms may influence this 
relationship. In the present study, patients with the CYP4F2*3 
rs2108622 TT genotype had a significantly higher plasma 
MK4 concentration than those with the CC/CT genotypes, 
whereas plasma PK concentration did not differ significantly 
between the genotype groups. Nevertheless, substantial 
interindividual variability in plasma VK concentrations was 
observed within the genotype groups. The VKORC1 rs9923231 
polymorphism, which affects VKOR activity, could also 
potentially influence plasma VK concentrations. 12,39) However, 
consistent with a previous report, 40) plasma PK and MK4 con -
centrations did not differ significantly according to VKORC1 
genotype in the present study. These findings highlight the 
difficulty of predicting plasma VK concentrations solely from 
genetic polymorphisms and are consistent with previous stud -
ies17,18,40,41) supporting the potential value of directly measuring 
plasma VK concentrations when evaluating the effects of VK.
Several studies have investigated the relationship between 
plasma VK concentrations and warfarin sensitivity. 17,18,42) 
Hirai et al .18) examined this association in 217 Japanese adult 
patients receiving warfarin therapy but found no significant 
correlation between plasma VK concentrations and warfarin 
sensitivity. In a separate study involving 37 pediatric patients, 
Hirai et al .17) found no association between warfarin sensitiv -
ity and plasma PK concentrations, although a weak negative 
correlation was observed with plasma MK4 concentrations. 
Similarly, in the present study, neither plasma PK nor MK4 
concentration was significantly correlated with warfarin 
sensitivity when analyzed as a continuous variable. In con -
trast, Kim et al .42) analyzed plasma PK concentrations in 203 
patients with atrial fibrillation and reported that patients with 
lower PK concentrations required more frequent PT-INR 
monitoring, potentially reflecting greater instability in antico -
agulation control. All patients presenting with gross hematuria 
in that study had low plasma PK concentrations (<0.4 ng/mL).  
Kwolek et al .43) described marked PT prolongation and sup -
pression of the VK-dependent coagulation pathway in a patient 
with gluten-sensitive enteropathy and VK deficiency, although 
plasma VK concentrations were not measured. Takada  
et al .44) reported markedly elevated PT-INR in a long-term 
warfarin user with a plasma PK concentration of 0.13 ng/mL.  
Taken together, these observations raise the possibility that 
the relationship between plasma VK concentration and 
anticoagulant response may become particularly relevant at 
low PK concentrations rather than following a simple linear  
concentration-dependent pattern across the entire range.
Our findings showed that plasma PK concentration 
<0.20 ng/mL was independently associated with higher war -
farin sensitivity, consistent with observations from previous 
studies. In healthy individuals, plasma VK concentrations 
have been reported to be 1.22 ± 0.57 ng/mL for PK and 
0.39 ± 0.46 ng/mL for MK4. 45) In contrast, patients receiving 
warfarin may exhibit lower VK concentrations because of 
enhanced VK metabolism and dietary VK restriction, with 
mean PK concentrations of 0.29–0.60 ng/mL and mean MK4 
concentrations of 0.10–0.36 ng/mL reported previously. 17,18,46) 
These observations support the potential relevance of evaluat -
ing low plasma PK concentrations in patients receiving warfa -
rin, including the exploratory cutoff of <0.20 ng/mL identified 
in the present study. Supporting this interpretation, Greer  
et al .47) reported that plasma PK concentrations <0.15 ng/mL 
were associated with elevated levels of protein induced by VK 
absence or antagonist-II, a marker of impaired γ-carboxylation 
of VK-dependent coagulation factors. Morris et al.48) reported 
that although the relationship between GGCX activity and 
VK concentration does not follow classical Michaelis–Menten 
kinetics, it exhibits a similar nonlinear, saturable pattern. 
This suggests that, at relatively sufficient VK concentrations, 
changes in VK availability may have a limited effect on 
GGCX-mediated γ-carboxylation, whereas at markedly low 
concentrations, limited VK availability may more substan -
tially limit this reaction. Under such substrate-limited condi -
tions, inhibition of VK recycling by warfarin could further 
reduce the availability of the reduced VK cofactor required 
for GGCX, resulting in less efficient γ-carboxylation of VK-  
dependent coagulation factors. Consequently, patients with 
markedly low plasma PK concentrations may exhibit higher 
PT-INR at a given warfarin concentration and thus higher 
WSI. Although this proposed mechanism was not directly 
evaluated in the present study, it may explain why the associ -
ation between plasma PK concentration and warfarin sensitiv -
ity was more apparent at low PK concentrations.
Although both PK and MK4 can serve as cofactors for 
GGCX in vitro , their effects on coagulation and tissue dis -
position may differ. 49) In VK-deficient rats, PK was at least 
twice as effective as MK4 in restoring coagulation factor 
synthesis.50) Differences in their tissue distribution and uti -
lization have also been reported, including greater hepatic
1683
Biol. Pharm. Bull. Vol. 49, No. 10 (2026)
accumulation of PK and more efficient utilization of MK4 
in extrahepatic vascular tissue. 51) Furthermore, the intrinsic 
clearance of MK4 epoxide reduction by human liver mic -
rosomes was reported to be approximately 30-fold higher 
than that of PK epoxide reduction, suggesting more efficient 
recycling of MK4. 52) Taken together, plasma PK and MK4 
concentrations may not equally reflect functional VK avail -
ability in the liver. Because PK is derived primarily from the 
diet and its intestinal absorption influences hepatic PK levels, 
plasma PK concentration may more directly reflect exogenous 
VK supply. 53) In contrast, plasma MK4 concentration may be 
influenced by its tissue distribution and utilization as well as 
efficient recycling. 51,52) These differences may partly explain 
why a clearer association with WSI was observed for PK than 
for MK4.
This study had several limitations. First, the patients 
included in this study were already receiving stable warfa -
rin therapy, and their exact PT-INR values before warfarin 
initiation could not be confirmed. Consequently, WSI was 
calculated assuming a pretreatment PT-INR of 1.00. However, 
because patients with liver cirrhosis or liver cancer, which may 
affect baseline coagulation status, were excluded, substantial 
elevation of PT-INR before warfarin initiation was considered 
unlikely. Second, the present study had limited power to eval -
uate interactions between low plasma PK status and genetic 
or clinical variables because of the small number of patients 
with low plasma PK concentrations and the limited sizes of 
the relevant genotype subgroups. Therefore, the observed 
association between low plasma PK concentration and warfa -
rin sensitivity should be interpreted as an average association 
across the study population, and whether this association 
differs according to genetic or clinical characteristics remains 
unclear. Furthermore, the interaction estimates obtained 
from the present cohort were imprecise, precluding a reliable 
estimation of the sample size required for future interaction 
analyses. Future studies with larger cohorts and prespecified 
interaction hypotheses are required to formally assess poten -
tial effect modification. Third, daily dietary VK intake was 
neither assessed nor controlled, and plasma concentrations of 
menaquinones other than MK4 and the composition of the gut 
microbiota were not evaluated. Because plasma PK concentra -
tion may be influenced by recent dietary VK intake, the extent 
to which dietary intake contributed to the observed plasma 
PK concentrations could not be determined. Furthermore, 
because the gut microbiota produce several menaquinones 
other than MK4, 54,55) t h e  p o t e n t i a l  e ff e c t s  o f  g u t  m i c r o b i o t a - 
derived menaquinones on warfarin sensitivity remain unclear. 
Fourth, this study analyzed the quinone form of VK, which is 
stable in blood. Ideally, the hydroquinone form of VK, which 
serves as the reduced cofactor for GGCX, 4,7,48) should also 
be evaluated. However, this form is chemically unstable and 
readily oxidized during sample handling, 56) making accurate 
quantification using conventional analytical techniques diffi -
cult. Future studies should therefore establish reliable methods 
for quantifying the hydroquinone form of VK and investigate 
the relationship between VK hydroquinone concentrations and 
coagulation activity, which may provide more direct insight 
into the role of VK status in warfarin sensitivity.
Plasma PK and MK4 concentrations were not signifi -
cantly correlated with warfarin sensitivity when analyzed 
as continuous variables. However, prediction modeling and 
correction–effect analysis indicated that low plasma PK 
concentration, particularly PK <0.20 ng/mL, provided addi -
tional information for WSI prediction. In multivariable linear 
regression analysis, plasma PK concentration <0.20 ng/mL 
was independently associated with higher WSI after adjust -
ment for established clinical and genetic factors, whereas 
MK4-based models showed weaker and less consistent con -
tributions. These findings suggest that direct measurement of 
plasma PK concentration may provide additional information 
for understanding interindividual variability in warfarin 
sensitivity beyond that explained by genetic polymorphisms 
alone. In particular, plasma PK measurement may help char -
acterize increased warfarin sensitivity in patients with sus -
pected low VK status, such as those with poor dietary intake 
or nutritional deficiency. Further studies are needed to vali -
date the clinically relevant range of plasma PK concentrations 
during warfarin therapy, including the exploratory <0.20 ng/
mL threshold identified in this study, and to establish strate -
gies for safely managing patients with markedly low plasma 
PK concentrations.

Clinical data and pharmacogenetic results were analysed from electronic medical records. The studied variants included CYP2C9 (2, 3) and VKORC1 (-1639G>A). [PMID 42862104] (American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists, 2026) Genotype-Guided Dosing Improves Attainment of Therapeutic Troughs in CYP3A5 Normal Metabolizers After Kidney Transplantation. CYP3A5 expressors experience delayed therapeutic tacrolimus concentrations after kidney transplantation, thus, requiring higher tacrolimus doses. Although genotype-guided dosing has demonstrated benefit with immediate-release tacrolimus, data evaluating tacrolimus extended-release (XR) formulations is limited. This retrospective, single-center cohort study included adult kidney transplant recipients with CYP3A5 normal or intermediate metabolizer phenotypes initiated on tacrolimus XR between November 2020 and August 2025. Patients received either conventional fixed-dose tacrolimus XR 4 mg daily or genotype-guided dosing (8 mg daily for normal metabolizers and 6 mg daily for intermediate metabolizers). The primary outcome was time to therapeutic tacrolimus trough concentration (≥8 ng/mL). Secondary outcomes included total dose adjustments, rate of supratherapeutic troughs, intrapatient variability, rejection rate, and renal function. Eighty-one patients met inclusion criteria, including 43 patients in the conventional dosing group and 38 patients in the genotype-guided group. Genotype-guided dosing significantly improved time to therapeutic troughs ≥8 in the normal metabolizers (median 13 vs 25 days; P=0.007), but not in the overall cohort. Both normal and intermediate metabolizers in the genotype-guided group demonstrated significantly higher tacrolimus trough concentrations that were closer to the therapeutic target on post-operative day 3. Genotype-guided dosing was not associated with an increased incidence of supratherapeutic tacrolimus concentrations or adverse clinical outcomes. [PMID 41357367 | PMC12679217 full text via pmc_xml] Impact of cytochrome P450 3A5 expression on clinical outcomes in renal transplant recipients receiving tacrolimus-based immunosuppression. :: Core Tip: This study evaluated the effect of cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A)5 polymorphism on tacrolimus pharmacokinetics and clinical outcomes in renal transplant recipients. CYP3A5 expressors required significantly higher tacrolimus doses than non-expressors from 6 months onward to maintain therapeutic levels. Non-expressors consistently showed higher tacrolimus trough concentration (ng/mL)/daily tacrolimus dose (mg/kg/day) ratios, reflecting slower drug metabolism. Despite these differences, no significant impact was seen on acute rejection rates, renal function, or complications such as new onset diabetes after transplantation and hypomagnesemia. These findings emphasize the importance of genotype-guided tacrolimus dosing for individualized immunosuppressive management, while therapeutic drug monitoring helps mitigate clinical variability, ensuring comparable outcomes between expressors and non-expressors.
The global burden of end-stage kidney disease is on the rise and successful kidney transplantation is the most effective kidney replacement therapy improving quality of life. Lifelong immunosuppressive therapy is required in kidney transplant recipients to prevent both early and late acute rejection episodes and chronic allograft dysfunction. The long-term outcome depends on achieving a balance between preventing rejection and minimizing drug-related toxicity through appropriate immunosuppressive regimens. Tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor which suppresses the T-cell function by inhibiting the synthesis of interleukin-2 and cytokines, thus preventing acute and chronic rejection[1]. Cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A)5 is the main enzyme for tacrolimus metabolism while there are some other enzymes and proteins with a minor role in its metabolism, including UDP-glucuronosyltransferases and P-glycoprotein. The tacrolimus trough levels with same dose vary significantly due to inter-individual variability in its metabolism by the genetic polymorphisms in the CYP3A5 gene belonging to cytochrome P450 3A enzyme system. Genetic variations in the CYP3A5 gene categorize patients into two metabolizer phenotypes: (1) Expressors (carrying at least one functional CYP3A51 allele); and (2) Non-expressors (homozygous for the non-functional CYP3A53/*3 genotype)[2]. Expressors exhibit higher CYP3A5 activity, leading to faster tacrolimus metabolism and potentially subtherapeutic drug levels if standard doses are administered, increasing the risk of graft rejection. Non-expressors have lower CYP3A5 activity, resulting in slower tacrolimus metabolism and a higher risk of over-immunosuppression and nephrotoxicity, infection, and metabolic complications such as diabetes or dyslipidemia[3].

paragraphs.text: CYP3A5 expressors experience delayed therapeutic tacrolimus concentrations after kidney transplantation, thus, requiring higher tacrolimus doses. Although genotype-guided dosing has demonstrated benefit with immediate-release tacrolimus, data evaluating tacrolimus extended-release (XR) formulations is limited. This retrospective, single-center cohort study included adult kidney transplant recipients with CYP3A5 normal or intermediate metabolizer phenotypes initiated on tacrolimus XR between November 2020 and August 2025. Patients received either conventional fixed-dose tacrolimus XR 4 mg daily or genotype-guided dosing (8 mg daily for normal metabolizers and 6 mg daily for intermediate metabolizers). Expressors received significantly higher doses of tacrolimus at the 6th and 12th month post-transplant compared to non-expressors, with no significant differences in trough levels during the early post-transplant period but higher levels from 6 months onwards. Paragraph 17 establishes that CYP3A5 polymorphism influences tacrolimus dosing in renal transplant recipients, with expressors requiring higher doses to maintain therapeutic drug levels compared to non-expressors. This highlights the importance of genotype-guided immunosuppressive strategies for optimal tacrolimus dosing.
