[PMID 42790941] (Annals of clinical and laboratory science, 2026) Rapid G6PD Screening Workflow for Timely Tumor Lysis Syndrome Management in Pediatric Oncology. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDD) poses significant safety concerns in pediatric oncology, particularly during tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) management where rasburicase may precipitate hemolysis or methemoglobinemia. Prior to this initiative, our institution relied on send-out quantitative G6PD testing with prolonged turnaround times (TAT), limiting timely clinical decision-making. A rapid, in-house qualitative G6PD screening assay with reflex quantitative testing for abnormal ("Intermediate" or "Deficient") results was implemented and incorporated into institutional TLS guidelines. Test utilization, TAT, and concordance between qualitative screening, quantitative enzyme activity, and World Health Organization (WHO) classification criteria were evaluated. A total of 106 patients underwent qualitative G6PD screening between August 2025 and March 2026. Average TAT was less than 7 hours across all campuses. Screening classified 7 patients as "Deficient," 56 as "Intermediate," and 43 as "Normal." 66 patients underwent quantitative testing, of whom 23 had enzyme activity below the age-specific reference range. These included all 7 patients classified as "Deficient" and 16 initially classified as "Intermediate." However, only 1 patient met WHO criteria for clinically significant G6PD deficiency (<30% activity). Rapid G6PD screening supported timely TLS management. Reflex quantitative testing remains essential, as interpretation varies substantially between qualitative screening, quantitative reference intervals, and WHO activity-based criteria.
[PMID 37748497 | PMC7615565 full text via pmc_xml] Primaquine dose and the risk of haemolysis in patients with uncomplicated Plasmodium vivax malaria: a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis. :: Research in context Evidence before this study We identified prospective studies and meta-analyses evaluating the effect of primaquine use and dose on the risk of haemolysis in patients with acute Plasmodium vivax malaria and normal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity (ie, ≥30% of the adjusted median value for healthy male individuals), published in any language from database inception to June 8, 2023, using the terms “vivax”, “primaquine”, and “haemolysis” in MEDLINE, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Central. An individual patient data meta-analysis including 1692 patients with normal G6PD activity found no difference in haemoglobin concentrations at the day of nadir for patients treated with or without primaquine, with no assessment of primaquine dose. A nested cohort study found that haemolysis after primaquine was greater in 33 female patients heterozygous for G6PD deficiency than in 198 patients with wild-type G6PD, with increased haemolysis in heterozygous patients after receiving 1 mg/kg per day of primaquine compared with 0·5 mg/kg per day. Added value of this study This individual patient data meta-analysis included data from 5462 patients with P vivax malaria with G6PD activity of 30% or higher, enrolled from 18 studies, and is the largest study to assess the risk of haemolysis with different primaquine daily doses. The results, co-published with an analysis of the effect of primaquine dose on treatment efficacy and tolerability, show similar mean haemoglobin concentrations at days 2–3 with and without primaquine use at a population level after adjustment for confounders. Severe haemolytic events were rare but more common after primaquine regimens at 1 mg/kg per day than after treatment without primaquine. Compared with patients with G6PD activity of 70% or higher, patients with G6PD activity between 30% and less than 70% had lower haemoglobin concentrations after treatment, with or without primaquine. Implications of all the available evidence Patients with G6PD activity of 30% or higher treated with primaquine regimens at 0·25 mg/kg per day and 0·5 mg/kg per day have a similar risk of haemolysis to those treated without primaquine, supporting the safe use of primaquine at these doses to prevent relapsing P vivax malaria.

[PMID 37347978] (Journal of interferon & cytokine research : the official journal of the International Society for Interferon and Cytokine Research, 2023) IFNL4 Genotype Frequencies in Asian Populations Support Shorter Duration Therapy with Sofosbuvir-Based Hepatitis C Virus Regimens to Increase the Number Cured. Globally, ∼56.8 million people are chronically infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV), with about half residing in Asia. The cost and efficiency of delivering regimens based on direct-acting antiviral agents for HCV are important considerations in implementing these curative treatments. For sofosbuvir-based regimens, most patients are treated for 12 weeks; however, treatment for 8 weeks has been shown to cure HCV infection in 95% of patients without cirrhosis. Furthermore, virological failure after 8-week treatment occurs in only 1%-2% of individuals without cirrhosis, who have a favorable IFNL4 genotype, which is present in >50% of South Asians and >80% of East Asians. We propose that sofosbuvir-based treatment for 8 weeks, or perhaps shorter, would yield high response rate regimens in Asian countries and markedly increase the number of patients who could be cured for a given cost of the medication. We propose that a noninferiority trial in an East Asian population be conducted to test this hypothesis.
[PMID 39216831 | PMC11490369 full text via pmc_xml] IFNL4 genotype and other personal characteristics to predict response to 8-week sofosbuvir-based treatment for chronic hepatitis C. :: Chronic infection with hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a leading global cause of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and end-stage liver disease. Treatment with a regimen of direct-acting antiviral agents (DAAs) yields a high rate of sustained virological response (SVR), which markedly reduces the risk of those outcomes. The availability of DAA treatments creates the opportunity to eliminate HCV as a global public health problem(1) and, in 2016, the World Health Assembly set 2030 global targets to diagnose 90% of individuals with chronic hepatitis C and to treat 80% of those who are diagnosed.(2) Presently, very few countries are on pace to meet those goals.(3-5) Globally, for 2015-2022, an estimated 36% of those with HCV infection had been diagnosed and only 20% had been treated.(6)
Although the cost of DAA regimens has dropped over the past 10 years, it remains a barrier to fuller treatment implementation in some countries.(4, 6-10) Sofosbuvir is the backbone of several widely used DAA regimens. For patients without cirrhosis, the standard duration of sofosbuvir-based treatment is 12 weeks, however, SVR rates >95% were achieved after 8-week treatment with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir(11) or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir.(12)
SVR rates are even higher among individuals with certain characteristics. Genotype for the IFNL4-ΔG/TT variant is associated with response to HCV treatment, with the IFNL4-TT allele, which abrogates production of the IFN-λ4 protein, being strongly associated with better response. Paradoxically, the best response to therapy is seen among individuals with the IFNL4-TT/TT genotype (i.e., those who cannot generate the IFN-λ4 protein at all). Previously, using limited data from clinical trials, we showed that genotype for IFNL4 rs12979860, which is a strong surrogate for the functional IFNL4-ΔG/TT (rs368234815) variant,(13) predicts response among patients treated for 8 weeks with either ledipasvir/sofosbuvir(11, 14) or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir regimen.(15) In addition, females had better response rates than males.(11, 14)

[PMID 42364973 | PMC13310184 full text via pmc_xml] PBPK Modeling and Clinical Data Reveal Reduced Impact of CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 Inhibitors on Elimination of Siponimod. :: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the leading cause of neurological disability among young adults and is the predominant disorder that causes demyelination in the central nervous system [1]. It often manifests as relapsing types, such as relapsing–remitting MS (RRMS) or secondary progressive MS (SPMS) [2].
Currently, a considerable medical need remains to find therapies that will be effective in delaying disability progression in patients with SPMS [2]. Siponimod is a potent and orally administered modulator that specifically targets sphingosine‐1‐phosphate (S1P) receptors [3]. It selectively attaches to two out of the five known G protein–coupled receptors on lymphocytes, consequently hindering their exit from lymph nodes. This reduces the recirculation of T cells into the central nervous system, resulting in reduced central inflammation [4, 5]. Siponimod is approved in more than 80 countries for the treatment of relapsing–remitting MS and active secondary progressive MS [6]. The polymorphic enzyme CYP2C9 is the major metabolizing enzyme for siponimod (79.3%), followed by CYP3A4 (18.5%), in subjects with the CYP2C9*1*1 genotype (extensive metabolizers) according to in vitro enzyme phenotyping data [7, 8]. The maintenance dose of siponimod in patients with CYP2C9 genotypes *1*1, *1*2 and *2*2 is 2 mg once daily and 1 mg for *3*3 and *2*3. The different genotypes require different titration when starting treatment with siponimod (Table S2).

Liver metabolic zonation enables hepatocytes to carry out diverse, spatially organized functions essential for liver homeostasis and metabolism. However, in vitro recapitulation of zone-specific diversity, particularly in human pluripotent stem cell (PSC)-derived hepatocyte-like cells (HLCs), remains challenging, as these cells typically exhibit an immature phenotype. Here, we report a scalable differentiation protocol for generating 3D organoids from PSCs with defined zone 1 (z1-HLCs) or zone 3 (z3-HLCs) identities. When benchmarked against primary human hepatocytes (PHHs), these HLCs exhibit zone-specific enhanced postnatal metabolic functions. z1-HLCs reveal high albumin and urea production, whereas z3-HLCs show elevated glutamine secretion and cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme activity, including CYP3A4, CYP1A2, and CYP2C9. Hallmarks of functional zonation were further confirmed via proteomics, transcriptomics, metabolic assays, and oxygen consumption. z3-HLCs show increased sensitivity to acetaminophen-induced cytotoxicity and distinct immune interactions with primary monocytes. Collectively, the zonated liver organoids provide a promising platform for studying zone-specific liver metabolism, drug metabolism, toxicology, and liver disease, including liver injury.

paper_digests.title: PBPK Modeling and Clinical Data Reveal Reduced Impact of CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 Inhibitors on Elimination of Siponimod.

paragraphs.text: Using the updated model, siponimod net AUC ratios ranging from 0.27 to 0.39 were predicted for the CYP2C9*1*1, *1*2, *1*3, *2*2, and *2*3 genotypes for the strong CYP3A4/moderate CYP2C9 inducer rifampicin. For the moderate CYP3A4 inducer efavirenz, siponimod was predicted to show no to weak induction effects, with net AUC ratios between 0.64 and 1.03. Therefore, strong CYP3A4 inducers should be avoided, and moderate CYP3A4 inducers should be used with caution.

The dose titration of siponimod is a necessary step to desensitize the S1P1 receptors in the heart, being most critical at treatment day 1. Using PBPK modeling, it was demonstrated that there is little difference between the C max values across CYP2C9 genotypes for the first day of treatment (Figure 4), which is considered most relevant for the desensitization with regard to cardiac safety at treatment initiation. Even in the presence of fluconazole, which represents the worst case DDI scenario for siponimod with the highest net DDI effect of CYP inhibitors, little difference in the C max concentrations across genotypes was predicted for the first day.

paragraphs.section: Performance Verification of the Updated Siponimod
paragraphs.text: Simulated plasma concentration profiles over time after single (0.1–75 mg) and multiple oral administrations (0.3–20 mg q.d. for 28 days) of siponimod matched the observed PK parameters. The prediction error of simulated C max and AUC values is presented in Figure 3, showing equal to or < 25% deviation. The DDI effect of fluconazole with observed siponimod C max and AUC ratios of 1.10 and 1.98 was well predicted with simulated ratios of 1.09 and 1.88, respectively (Table S11). All observed and simulated PK profiles were comparable. Similarly, for rifampicin, a DDI effect on siponimod was observed with C max and AUC ratios 0.55 and 0.43; the predicted values were 0.46 and 0.32, respectively (Table S12).

For the four CYP inhibitors, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, erythromycin, and fluconazole, the DDI simulations with siponimod were performed (Table S12). The maximal predicted exposure increase (excluding genotype CYP2C9*3*3) was 1.12 for the genotype CYP2C9*2*3 with the strong CYP3A4 inhibitor ketoconazole and 1.88 for CYP2C9 wild type for the dual moderate CYP2C9/CYP3A4 inhibitor fluconazole. Calculation of the net DDI effect based on AUC factoring in the genotype‐specific exposure and the genotype‐specific dose (Table 2). The net AUC ratios were close to 1 for the CYP3A4 inhibitors clarithromycin, ketoconazole, and erythromycin and ranging from 1.66 to 2.20 for the moderate CYP2C9/CYP3A4 inhibitor fluconazole across genotypes.

The first day of treatment is critical for cardiac safety, with little difference in Cmax across CYP2C9 genotypes even under strong inhibitors like fluconazole. The paper discusses the drug-drug interaction (DDI) effects of CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 inhibitors on siponimod. It mentions that fluconazole, a dual moderate CYP2C9/CYP3A4 inhibitor, increases siponimod exposure with an AUC ratio ranging from 1.66 to 2.20 across genotypes. Rifampicin and efavirenz, as inducers of CYP3A4, moderately decrease siponimod exposure. The updated PBPK model predicts that siponimod is minimally affected by strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and moderately affected by fluconazole. paper_digests.title: Ocular safety signals of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators in postmarketing surveillance.

paragraphs.text: Siponimod contributed 8,263 primary suspect reports and 677 ocular adverse event reports, with an ocular reporting proportion of 8.2%. The most frequently reported ocular PTs were visual impairment (n = 245), vision blurred (n = 208), macular oedema (n = 62), eye pain (n = 60), diplopia (n = 42), and eye disorder (n = 40). The highest ROR estimates were observed for macular oedema (n = 62; ROR, 34.23; 95% CI, 26.60–44.05), photopsia (n = 13; ROR, 6.90; 95% CI, 4.04–11.79), ocular discomfort (n = 28; ROR, 5.01; 95% CI, 3.46–7.24), diplopia (n = 42; ROR, 4.89; 95% CI, 3.61–6.61), and visual impairment (n = 245; ROR, 4.82; 95% CI, 4.24–5.47). paper_digests.title: Effects of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators on remyelination in multiple sclerosis: evidence from in vitro experiments, animal models and human studies.

paragraphs.text: Fostering remyelination pathways in vivo remains a major challenge of MS care: despite multiple efforts and several clinical trials, there are currently no molecules approved with the indication of promoting myelin repair in PwMS. In this scenario, it is of great interest to explore the remyelination potential of known DMT with a broader spectrum of action, going beyond immune modulation, such as the S1P modulators. The four drugs of this class approved for the treatment of MS differ substantially in their receptor selectivity profiles, which likely influence their remyelinating properties. Fingolimod is a non-selective modulator with activity at S1PR1, S1PR3, S1PR4, and S1PR5. Its broad receptor profile contributes to robust remyelinating effects mediated primarily through S1PR1, S1PR3 an

On a therapeutic viewpoint, a class of compounds modulating S1P receptors has been developed in the field of multiple sclerosis (MS) and represented a major advance in the treatment landscape, with fingolimod being the first oral immune-active MS therapy approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), dating back to September 2010. These agents act as functional antagonists of the target receptors, by inducing S1PR internalization and degradation, particularly affecting S1P1 on lymphocytes, thereby preventing lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs and reducing CNS infiltration. Four S1P modulators are currently used for MS treatment: fingolimod (Gilenya®), siponimod (Mayzent®), ozanimod (Zeposia®), and ponesimod (Ponvory®). Fingolimod (FTY720) was the pioneer of this class of molecules

In EAE, exposure to ozanimod reduced inflammation, demyelination and neurodegeneration. In the cuprizone mice, ozanimod prevented axonal degradation and myelin loss but did not enhance remyelination after intoxication and toxin withdrawal, likely due to the exclusive S1P1 receptor engagement by free drug in this model, while the remyelinating effect is mediated by S1P5 receptor (44). Indeed, the authors highlighted that ozanimod has limited activity at mouse S1P5 compared with human S1P5, suggesting that rodent studies may underestimate potential human S1P5-mediated effects on oligodendrocyte biology.

paper_digests.summary: Paragraph 36 discusses the pharmacological properties of siponimod, a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator used in multiple sclerosis (MS) treatment. It highlights that siponimod selectively activates S1PR1 and S1PR5 receptors to promote remyelination without mentioning specific genes for a pharmacogenetics panel. Siponimod is a second-generation, selective S1P receptor modulator approved for active secondary progressive MS. It acts on S1PR1 and S1PR5 subtypes to maintain immunomodulatory efficacy while potentially enhancing CNS effects. Paragraph 34 discusses ozanimod's effects in animal models, suggesting that its remyelination properties may be mediated by S1P5 receptor engagement. However, it also notes that rodent studies might underestimate human S1P5-mediated effects due to species differences.

[PMID 42549153 | PMC13430968 full text via pmc_xml] Rifampin-induced fluvastatin toxicity: a case report and review of literature. :: Fluvastatin, a low- to moderate-intensity lipid-lowering 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase inhibitor, is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of familial hypercholesterolemia, homozygous in adults and heterozygous in patients aged ≥10 years, and for reducing the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease as both primary and secondary prevention [1]. Additionally, statins are recommended to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality risk in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) [2].
Although almost completely absorbed (>90%), indicating minimal intestinal metabolism and limited efflux, fluvastatin oral bioavailability ranges from 19–29% due to extensive first-pass hepatic extraction mediated primarily by the rate-limiting hepatic influx transporter, organic anion transporting polypeptide 1B1 (OATP1B1). Subsequently, it is predominantly metabolized (>80%) by cytochrome P450 2C9 (CYP2C9) [3]. Decreased-function polymorphisms in solute carrier organic anion transporter 1B1 (SLCO1B1), which encodes OATP1B1, and CYP2C9 are associated with increased fluvastatin systemic exposure and reduction of its maximum tolerated dose [4].
Rifampin is an essential antimicrobial used in the management of several serious infections, including prosthetic valve infective endocarditis caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci and tuberculosis [5]. As a potent inducer of multiple CYPs, uridine 5′-diphospho-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs), and ATP-binding cassette (ABC) efflux transporters [5], rifampin is a major perpetrator of numerous drug–drug interactions, mainly reducing systemic exposure of substrates, including statins, to extremely low levels [1, 6–11]. However, it is also a strong competitive inhibitor of the predominant hepatic statin influx transporter OATP1B1, which may result in increased statin concentrations [11–21]. These opposing effects, described in multiple pharmacokinetic studies [1, 6–21], make rifampin interaction with statins difficult to manage, as they may result in either markedly reduced or elevated statin levels, leading to either attenuation of lipid-lowering effect or increased risk of muscle toxicity, respectively.
Specifically, rifampin induces CYP2C9 transcription by activating its key de novo synthesis regulatory nuclear receptor, pregnane X receptor, thereby increasing its mRNA expression rate up to six-fold [5]. However, the time course required for CYP2C9 induction ranges from two to more than 4 weeks for maximal effect, which can delay the need for fluvastatin dose escalation [5, 22]. Conversely, there is evidence that single-dose and simultaneous rifampin co-administration with fluvastatin can significantly increase fluvastatin exposure [14, 16].
This report aims to describe a case of rifampin-induced fluvastatin toxicity following the addition of anti-tuberculous therapy in a patient who had been receiving chronic fluvastatin treatment.

[PMID 40107569] (European journal of pharmaceutical sciences : official journal of the European Federation for Pharmaceutical Sciences, 2025) Comparative uptake of statins by hepatic organic anion transporting polypeptides. Uptake into hepatocytes by the organic anion transporting polypeptides (OATP) 1B1, 1B3, and 2B1 can form a rate-determining step in drug clearance. While several lipid-lowering statin drugs are substrates of the hepatic OATPs, the literature statin uptake profiles form a wide range with values obtained from different laboratories and systems. Therefore, this study aimed to characterize hepatic OATP-mediated transport of statins in a single-laboratory experimental setup, allowing comparison between the statins and OATPs. The uptake of atorvastatin, 3R,5S-fluvastatin, 3S,5R-fluvastatin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin, and simvastatin acid was assessed in human embryonic kidney 293 cells overexpressing OATP1B1, 1B3, or OATP2B1. All the three OATPs transported atorvastatin with Km values 2.6 μM (1B1), 1.9 μM (1B3), and 1.1 μM (2B1). Also rosuvastatin was transported by all the OATPs: OATP1B1 (as previously reported from our lab) and 2B1 affinities were similar (13 μM) while OATP1B3 had a Km of 40 μM. Although all OATPs also transported pravastatin, the uptake by OATP2B1 was not saturated at the studied concentration range, and affinity parameters could be determined only for OATP1B1 and 1B3 at Km 37 μM and 28 µM, respectively. OATP2B1 was the high-affinity transporter of the fluvastatin enantiomers (Km 0.57 μM for 3S,5R- and 2.5 μM for 3R,5S-fluvastatin) which were not taken up by OATP1B3. Importantly, active simvastatin acid uptake was observed only for OATP1B1 with a Km value of 2.1 μM. Taken together, only OATP1B1 could transport all statins and, in general, the affinities of the hydrophobic statins (atorvastatin, fluvastatin, simvastatin acid) were higher compared to the hydrophilic statins (pravastatin, rosuvastatin). In the case of fluvastatin, CYP2C9 variants may, additionally, lead to excessive exposure while using simultaneous rifampin, particularly at the initiation phase of the latter, when influx transporter inhibition precedes full metabolizing enzyme induction.

paragraphs.text: Optical isomers of fluvastatin RR, RS and SS displayed dose-dependent antagonistic activity against GR, which is a master regulator of xenobiotic metabolic pathways by multiple mechanisms, including the regulation of PXR expression. Antiglucocorticoid activity of 3R5R-fluvastatin and 3S5S-fluvastatin was also confirmed in human hepatocytes, where we observed down-regulation of TAT mRNA by these two compounds. Therefore, the induction of P450s by fluvastatin comprises both agonist effects on PXR and antagonist effects on GR. [PMID 42862104] (American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists, 2026) Genotype-Guided Dosing Improves Attainment of Therapeutic Troughs in CYP3A5 Normal Metabolizers After Kidney Transplantation. CYP3A5 expressors experience delayed therapeutic tacrolimus concentrations after kidney transplantation, thus, requiring higher tacrolimus doses. Although genotype-guided dosing has demonstrated benefit with immediate-release tacrolimus, data evaluating tacrolimus extended-release (XR) formulations is limited. This retrospective, single-center cohort study included adult kidney transplant recipients with CYP3A5 normal or intermediate metabolizer phenotypes initiated on tacrolimus XR between November 2020 and August 2025. Patients received either conventional fixed-dose tacrolimus XR 4 mg daily or genotype-guided dosing (8 mg daily for normal metabolizers and 6 mg daily for intermediate metabolizers). The primary outcome was time to therapeutic tacrolimus trough concentration (≥8 ng/mL). Secondary outcomes included total dose adjustments, rate of supratherapeutic troughs, intrapatient variability, rejection rate, and renal function. Eighty-one patients met inclusion criteria, including 43 patients in the conventional dosing group and 38 patients in the genotype-guided group. Genotype-guided dosing significantly improved time to therapeutic troughs ≥8 in the normal metabolizers (median 13 vs 25 days; P=0.007), but not in the overall cohort. Both normal and intermediate metabolizers in the genotype-guided group demonstrated significantly higher tacrolimus trough concentrations that were closer to the therapeutic target on post-operative day 3. Genotype-guided dosing was not associated with an increased incidence of supratherapeutic tacrolimus concentrations or adverse clinical outcomes. [PMID 42904383] (Drug metabolism reviews, 2026) Schisandrol A and Schisandrol B from Schisandra chinensis: Drug Metabolism, Transporter Interactions, and Herb-Drug Interaction Potential. Schisandrol A (Sch A) and Schisandrol B (Sch B) are structurally related dibenzocyclooctadiene lignans from Schisandra chinensis, but their drug-metabolism and interaction profiles are not interchangeable. This review critically evaluates their absorption, distribution, metabolism, transporter interactions, nuclear-receptor regulation, and herb-drug interaction potential, with particular emphasis on the distinction between purified compounds and multi-lignan botanical preparations. Oral exposure is strongly formulation dependent. In rats, purified Sch B shows substantially lower absolute bioavailability than Sch B administered within S. chinensis extract, whereas available Sch A studies likewise indicate considerable effects of formulation on systemic exposure. CYP3A4 is a major oxidative pathway for both compounds, although Sch B shows a more prominent interaction liability through reversible and time-dependent CYP3A inhibition. Both lignans can modulate P-glycoprotein function, but available transport studies do not support their blanket classification as conventional P-glycoprotein substrates. Sch B additionally activates pregnane X receptor signaling, creating a mechanistic distinction between acute enzyme inhibition and potential induction during repeated exposure. Animal drug-interaction studies and physiologically based pharmacokinetic models support interaction potential, while clinical evidence is strongest for multi-lignan Wuzhi preparations that alter tacrolimus disposition. Direct human evidence remains limited, particularly for purified Sch B and repeated-dose compound-specific interaction studies. (2019) demonstrated that the heterozygous or homozygous variant genotypes in rs2032582 also result in higher plasma concentrations. Zhu et al. (2020), on the other hand, demonstrated an association of the wild-type (CC) genotype in the rs1128503 and rs2032582 polymorphisms with a higher probability of subtherapeutic plasma concentrations of TAC. Despite this finding, other studies indicate the absence of significant associations between ABCB1 gene polymorphisms and plasma levels (Ho et al., 2024; Khaled et al., 2016; Seligson et al., 2024), C/D ratio (Khaled et al., 2016; Pasternak et al., 2022).

Finally, regarding the clinical outcomes evaluated in the studies, AKI (Khaled et al., 2016; Seligson et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2020), TMA (Khaled et al., 2016) or OS, RFS and NRM (Ho et al., 2024) were not influenced by ABCB1 polymorphisms. Only the study by Hamadeh et al. (2019) highlighted that carriers of homozygous variant genotypes for rs2032582 have a higher risk of toxicity associated with the use of TAC.

This is the first systematic review to investigate the influence of genetic polymorphisms on the pharmacokinetics and/or outcomes of CNIs (TAC and CSA), especially in HCT recipients. Eleven studies were included, mostly retrospective and conducted in the USA, with the majority focusing on TAC, and only two addressing CSA. We highlight the significant impact of the CYP3A5 rs776746 polymorphism on the pharmacokinetics of TAC, such as TAC levels, C/D ratio or therapeutic index, and on clinical outcomes, such as AKI and GVHD. In contrast, polymorphisms in CYP3A4 and ABCB1 showed less consistent results, evidencing a variability in the impact of these genes on pharmacokinetic and clinical parameters.

The studies included in this review that investigated polymorphisms in the CYP3A5 gene unanimously demonstrated the influence of these polymorphisms on pharmacokinetics and/or clinical outcome mainly related to TAC. Final parameter estimates demonstrated high precision and are summarized in Table 3. The typical population value for CL/F was 23.61 L/h. Quantitatively, fluconazole co‐administration exerted a dominant inhibitory effect, reducing drug clearance by 33% (95% CI: 30%–36%), whereas prednisolone induced a modest increase of 8% (95% CI: 3%–13%). Warfarin is an anticoagulant used to prevent thromboembolic events, such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), and atrial fibrillation. It works by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase complex 1 (VKORC1) activity, thereby reducing the production of active clotting factors. Genetic polymorphisms in VKORC1 (-1639G>A, rs9923231) and CYP2C9 (430C>T, rs1799853; 1075A>C, rs1057910) significantly influence warfarin metabolism. These genetic variations can lead to substantial interindividual variability in warfarin dosing requirements. For instance, individuals with VKORC1 variant alleles may require lower doses of warfarin due to increased sensitivity to the drug, while those with CYP2C9 variants may metabolize warfarin more rapidly, necessitating higher doses.

Clinical factors such as age, body surface area (BSA), amiodarone use, smoking status, and ethnicity also contribute to dose variability. For example, older patients typically require lower doses due to decreased hepatic metabolism, while those with larger BSA may need higher doses because of increased drug distribution volume.

Routine monitoring of the international normalized ratio (INR) is crucial for adjusting warfarin dosing to maintain therapeutic levels (2.0–3.0). Pharmacogenetic dosing algorithms based on multiple linear regression models incorporating genetic and clinical factors have been developed to optimize initial warfarin doses, thereby improving time in therapeutic range (%TTR) and reducing adverse events.

However, the performance of these pharmacogenetic algorithms can vary across different ethnic groups due to differences in allele frequencies. For instance, African American patients may exhibit lower %TTR with certain dosing algorithms compared to European patients, highlighting the need for personalized approaches based on genetic background.

Warfarin sensitivity exhibits marked interindividual variability, partly explained by genetic polymor -
phisms affecting vitamin K (VK) metabolism. However, the association between plasma VK concentrations 
and warfarin sensitivity remains unclear. We investigated this association in Japanese patients receiving 
warfarin therapy. Blood samples from patients aged ≥20 years were analyzed for genetic polymorphisms 
associated with warfarin sensitivity, warfarin concentrations, and plasma concentrations of phylloquinone 
(PK) and menaquinone-4 (MK4). The warfarin sensitivity index (WSI) was calculated as the change in pro -
thrombin time-international normalized ratio per S-warfarin-equivalent concentration. Among 105 patients, 
plasma PK and MK4 concentrations were not significantly correlated with WSI when analyzed as continuous 
variables ( p = 0.297 and p = 0.118, respectively). To determine whether plasma VK concentrations provided 
additional predictive information, WSI prediction models with and without VK variables were compared. 
Incorporating an indicator of plasma PK concentration <0.20 ng/mL improved model performance, whereas 
MK4-based models showed no clear improvement. In multivariable analysis, a plasma PK concentration 
<0.20 ng/mL was independently associated with a higher WSI after adjustment for established clinical and 
genetic factors (B = 0.703, 95% confidence interval, 0.057–1.349; p = 0.033). These findings suggest that a low 
plasma PK concentration may explain some of the interindividual variability in warfarin sensitivity beyond 
that accounted for by genetic polymorphisms. Direct measurement of plasma PK may provide additional 
information for understanding increased warfarin sensitivity in patients with low VK status.
Key words warfarin, phylloquinone, menaquinone-4, vitamin K

INTRODUCTION
Warfarin has been widely used for the prevention and 
treatment of thromboembolic disorders 1–3); however, marked 
interindividual variability in anticoagulant response remains 
an important clinical issue. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K 
epoxide reductase (VKOR), thereby disrupting the vitamin K 
(VK) cycle, reducing the activity of γ-glutamyl carboxylase 
(GGCX), and ultimately suppressing the activation of VK-  
dependent coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X. 4–7) Warfarin 
is administered as a racemic mixture of R- and S-enantiomers; 
the more potent S-enantiomer is metabolized predominantly 
by CYP2C9, whereas CYP2C19 contributes to the metabolism 
of the R-enantiomer.8,9) VK is recycled through the VK cycle 
involving VKOR, whereas CYP4F2 contributes to VK catab -
olism.5,6,10,11) Accordingly, genetic polymorphisms in enzymes 
and proteins involved in warfarin and VK metabolism,

Reduced VK serves as an essential cofactor for GGCX-

coagulation factors. 4–7) VK occurs in several forms, including 
phylloquinone (PK; vitamin K1), which is obtained mainly 
from green leafy vegetables, and menaquinone-4 (MK4), 
a vitamin K2 homologue found mainly in animal-derived 
foods.6,24) Although VK supplementation has been associated 
with warfarin efficacy and prothrombin time-international 
normalized ratio (PT-INR) variability, 24–36) the concentration–
response relationship between plasma VK concentrations and 
warfarin efficacy in humans remains unexplored. Furthermore, 
the extent to which VKORC1 and CYP4F2 polymorphisms 
influence VK pharmacokinetics is not fully understood. 
Therefore, relying solely on genetic polymorphism analysis 
may be insufficient to assess the contribution of VK pharma -
cokinetics to interindividual variability in warfarin efficacy.
To better understand individual differences in warfarin 
efficacy beyond those explained by plasma warfarin concen -
trations, evaluating VK status may provide additional insight. 
Accordingly, we conducted an integrated analysis of plasma 
VK concentrations together with genetic and nongenetic fac -
tors influencing warfarin sensitivity. The primary aim of this 
study was to investigate the association between plasma VK 
concentrations and warfarin sensitivity.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Study Population This study included Japanese patients aged 
≥20 years who were receiving warfarin therapy at the Department 
of Cardiology, Gunma University Hospital, or the Department of 
Internal Medicine, Japan Community Health Care Organization 
(JCHO) Gunma Chuo Hospital. Patients without PT-INR mea -
surements and those with cirrhosis or liver cancer were excluded. 
Whole blood samples were used for genetic polymorphism anal-
ysis, and plasma samples were used to determine the S-warfarin, 
R-warfarin, PK, and MK4 concentrations. Patient demographics, 
warfarin dosages, and laboratory data were obtained from elec -
tronic medical records. The study population overlapped with that 
of a previous study,23) except for three patients who were excluded 
because of insufficient plasma samples for warfarin and VK 
analyses. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Com -
mittee of Takasaki University of Health and Welfare (approval no. 
2338), the Ethics Committee of Gunma University (approval no. 
HS2020-170), and the Ethics Committee of JCHO Gunma Chuo 
Hospital (approval no. 2022-009), and the study was conducted 
in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed 
consent was obtained from all patients.
Genotype Detection  Genomic DNA was extracted from 
whole blood using the QIAamp ® Blood Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, 
CA, U.S.A.). Seven single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) 
were analyzed using TaqMan genotyping assays (Applied 
Biosystems, Foster City, CA, U.S.A.): VKORC1 rs9923231, 
CYP2C9*3 (rs1057910), CYP4F2*3 (rs2108622), CYP2C19*2 
(rs4244285), CYP2C19*3 (rs4986893), GGCX rs699664, and 
GGCX rs12714145. TaqMan primer and probe sets for each 
SNP allele were included in the kits. The specific assays 
used were as follows: VKORC1 rs9923231, C__30403261_20; 
CYP2C9*3 rs1057910, C_ _27104892_10; CYP4F2*3 rs2108622, 
C__16179493_40; CYP2C19*2 rs4244285, C__25986767_70; 
CYP2C19*3 rs4986893, C__27861809_10; GGCX rs699664, 
C_ _1036123_10; and GGCX rs12714145, C_ _31839079_10. 
TaqMan assays were performed using an Mx3000P instrument 
(Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, U.S.A.) according to 
the PCR cycling conditions recommended by Applied Biosys -
tems. CYP2C19 metabolizer status was categorized as rapid 
metabolizer (*1/*1), intermediate metabolizer (*1/*2 or *1/*3), 
or poor metabolizer (*2/*2, *2/*3, or *3/*3).
Sample Preparation of Warfarin and VK Sample pre -
treatment for warfarin quantification was performed according 
to the method described by Putriana et al .37) Briefly, 100 µL 
of plasma was mixed with 10 µL of a 0.5 -µg/mL griseofulvin 
solution as the internal standard, followed by the addition 
of 500 µL of acetonitrile. After vortex mixing, the sample 
was centrifuged at 13000 rpm for 4 min at 4°C. The resulting 
supernatant was evaporated to dryness under reduced pres -
sure, and the residue was reconstituted in 100 µL of the mobile 
phase before HPLC with fluorescence detection (HPLC-FLR) 
analysis.
Sample pretreatment for VK quantification was performed 
according to the method described by Ohno et al .,38) with 
PK-13C6 and MK4- 13C6 used as internal standards for PK and 
MK4, respectively. Briefly, 50 µL of an internal standard solution 
containing PK-13C6 and MK4- 13C6 at 5 ng/mL each was added 
to 0.4 mL of plasma, followed by the addition of 2 mL of etha -
nol. After vortex mixing for 1 min, 6 mL of hexane was added. 
The sample was vigorously shaken for 5 min and centrifuged at 
3000 rpm for 10 min. The upper hexane layer was collected and 
evaporated to dryness under reduced pressure. The residue was 
reconstituted in 100 µL of methanol before ultra-performance 
LC–MS analysis. All sample preparation procedures were per -
formed under protection from light.
HPLC with Fluorescence Detection Conditions for 
Warfarin S-warfarin and R-warfarin concentrations were 
determined using HPLC-FLR. LC and fluorescence detec -
tion were performed using an LC-20AD system (Shimadzu 
Corporation, Kyoto, Japan) and an RF-20A XS fluorescence 
detector (Shimadzu Corporation), respectively. Separation was 
achieved using a Chiralcel OD-RH column (4.6 × 150 mm; 
Daicel Chemical Industries, Tokyo, Japan). The LC conditions 
were as follows: column temperature, 40°C; mobile phase, an 
isocratic mixture of 65% 2 mM phosphate buffer (pH 2.0) and 
35% acetonitrile; flow rate, 0.5 mL/min; and injection volume, 
25 µL. Fluorescence detection was performed at excitation 
and emission wavelengths of 310 and 350 nm, respectively, for 
warfarin and 310 and 400 nm, respectively, for griseofulvin.

CYP4F2*3 rs2108622). Comorbid cancer was not included in 
the final model because only three patients had comorbid can -
cer. As a sensitivity analysis, multivariable linear regression 
analysis was repeated using the same explanatory variables 
after excluding these three patients. An additional model was 
constructed in which plasma PK and MK4 concentrations 
were simultaneously entered as continuous variables. All sta -
tistical analyses were performed using SPSS software, version 
26.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, U.S.A.), and exploratory spline-
based analyses were performed using Python (Python Soft -
ware Foundation, Wilmington, DE, U.S.A.). A p-value <0.05 
was considered statistically significant.

Factors Associated with Individual Differences in 
WSI The results of the multivariable linear regression anal -
ysis are presented in Table 6 . The model included plasma 
PK concentration dichotomized at 0.20 ng/mL, VKORC1

analyses: age, height, sex, eGFR, and CYP4F2*3 rs2108622.

plasma VK concentrations and warfarin sensitivity, which 
remains poorly understood. Although plasma PK and MK4 
concentrations showed negative correlations with WSI, these 
associations were not statistically significant when the con -
centrations were analyzed as continuous variables. However,

prediction modeling showed that incorporating an indicator 
of low plasma PK concentration, defined as PK <0.20 ng/mL, 
improved WSI prediction compared with the VK-free base 
model. In contrast, models incorporating PK as a continu -
ous variable or spline term and MK4-based models showed 
limited or no improvement. Visualization of the VK-related 
correction effects showed that the contribution of PK was most 
pronounced at low plasma concentrations and approached zero 
at approximately 0.20 ng/mL. An additional analysis using 
PT-INR as the outcome showed a similar pattern. Further -
more, multivariable linear regression analysis demonstrated 
that plasma PK concentration <0.20 ng/mL was independently 
associated with higher WSI after adjustment for established 
clinical and genetic factors. Collectively, these findings sug -
gest that the association between plasma PK concentration and 
warfarin sensitivity may be more apparent at low PK concen -
trations than across the entire concentration range.
Plant-derived PK, as a component of dietary VK, can influ -
ence warfarin sensitivity. 16,21,24–36) Specifically, in warfarin-  
treated patients with stable PT-INR, daily PK intakes of 
150 µg for women and 200 µg for men have been reported to 
significantly reduce mean INR. 27) Other studies have reported 
that a PK intake of 100–200 µg/d may help maintain PT-INR 
within the therapeutic range. 16,27,29,31–35) Conversely, Tanaka  
et al .21) demonstrated that VK intake independently contrib -
uted to the warfarin maintenance dose, although its effect was 
small. They suggested that factors such as VK synthesis by 
the gut microbiota and variability in VK metabolism associ -
ated with CYP4F2 genetic polymorphisms may influence this 
relationship. In the present study, patients with the CYP4F2*3 
rs2108622 TT genotype had a significantly higher plasma 
MK4 concentration than those with the CC/CT genotypes, 
whereas plasma PK concentration did not differ significantly 
between the genotype groups. Nevertheless, substantial 
interindividual variability in plasma VK concentrations was 
observed within the genotype groups. The VKORC1 rs9923231 
polymorphism, which affects VKOR activity, could also 
potentially influence plasma VK concentrations. 12,39) However, 
consistent with a previous report, 40) plasma PK and MK4 con -
centrations did not differ significantly according to VKORC1 
genotype in the present study. These findings highlight the 
difficulty of predicting plasma VK concentrations solely from 
genetic polymorphisms and are consistent with previous stud -
ies17,18,40,41) supporting the potential value of directly measuring 
plasma VK concentrations when evaluating the effects of VK.
Several studies have investigated the relationship between 
plasma VK concentrations and warfarin sensitivity. 17,18,42) 
Hirai et al .18) examined this association in 217 Japanese adult 
patients receiving warfarin therapy but found no significant 
correlation between plasma VK concentrations and warfarin 
sensitivity. In a separate study involving 37 pediatric patients, 
Hirai et al .17) found no association between warfarin sensitiv -
ity and plasma PK concentrations, although a weak negative 
correlation was observed with plasma MK4 concentrations. 
Similarly, in the present study, neither plasma PK nor MK4 
concentration was significantly correlated with warfarin 
sensitivity when analyzed as a continuous variable. In con -
trast, Kim et al .42) analyzed plasma PK concentrations in 203 
patients with atrial fibrillation and reported that patients with 
lower PK concentrations required more frequent PT-INR 
monitoring, potentially reflecting greater instability in antico -
agulation control. All patients presenting with gross hematuria 
in that study had low plasma PK concentrations (<0.4 ng/mL).  
Kwolek et al .43) described marked PT prolongation and sup -
pression of the VK-dependent coagulation pathway in a patient 
with gluten-sensitive enteropathy and VK deficiency, although 
plasma VK concentrations were not measured. Takada  
et al .44) reported markedly elevated PT-INR in a long-term 
warfarin user with a plasma PK concentration of 0.13 ng/mL.  
Taken together, these observations raise the possibility that 
the relationship between plasma VK concentration and 
anticoagulant response may become particularly relevant at 
low PK concentrations rather than following a simple linear  
concentration-dependent pattern across the entire range.
Our findings showed that plasma PK concentration 
<0.20 ng/mL was independently associated with higher war -
farin sensitivity, consistent with observations from previous 
studies. In healthy individuals, plasma VK concentrations 
have been reported to be 1.22 ± 0.57 ng/mL for PK and 
0.39 ± 0.46 ng/mL for MK4. 45) In contrast, patients receiving 
warfarin may exhibit lower VK concentrations because of 
enhanced VK metabolism and dietary VK restriction, with 
mean PK concentrations of 0.29–0.60 ng/mL and mean MK4 
concentrations of 0.10–0.36 ng/mL reported previously. 17,18,46) 
These observations support the potential relevance of evaluat -
ing low plasma PK concentrations in patients receiving warfa -
rin, including the exploratory cutoff of <0.20 ng/mL identified 
in the present study. Supporting this interpretation, Greer  
et al .47) reported that plasma PK concentrations <0.15 ng/mL 
were associated with elevated levels of protein induced by VK 
absence or antagonist-II, a marker of impaired γ-carboxylation 
of VK-dependent coagulation factors. Morris et al.48) reported 
that although the relationship between GGCX activity and 
VK concentration does not follow classical Michaelis–Menten 
kinetics, it exhibits a similar nonlinear, saturable pattern. 
This suggests that, at relatively sufficient VK concentrations, 
changes in VK availability may have a limited effect on 
GGCX-mediated γ-carboxylation, whereas at markedly low 
concentrations, limited VK availability may more substan -
tially limit this reaction. Under such substrate-limited condi -
tions, inhibition of VK recycling by warfarin could further 
reduce the availability of the reduced VK cofactor required 
for GGCX, resulting in less efficient γ-carboxylation of VK-  
dependent coagulation factors. Consequently, patients with 
markedly low plasma PK concentrations may exhibit higher 
PT-INR at a given warfarin concentration and thus higher 
WSI. Although this proposed mechanism was not directly 
evaluated in the present study, it may explain why the associ -
ation between plasma PK concentration and warfarin sensitiv -
ity was more apparent at low PK concentrations.
Although both PK and MK4 can serve as cofactors for 
GGCX in vitro , their effects on coagulation and tissue dis -
position may differ. 49) In VK-deficient rats, PK was at least 
twice as effective as MK4 in restoring coagulation factor 
synthesis.50) Differences in their tissue distribution and uti -
lization have also been reported, including greater hepatic

Biol. Pharm. Bull. Vol. 49, No. 10 (2026)
accumulation of PK and more efficient utilization of MK4 
in extrahepatic vascular tissue. 51) Furthermore, the intrinsic 
clearance of MK4 epoxide reduction by human liver mic -
rosomes was reported to be approximately 30-fold higher 
than that of PK epoxide reduction, suggesting more efficient 
recycling of MK4. 52) Taken together, plasma PK and MK4 
concentrations may not equally reflect functional VK avail -
ability in the liver. Because PK is derived primarily from the 
diet and its intestinal absorption influences hepatic PK levels, 
plasma PK concentration may more directly reflect exogenous 
VK supply. 53) In contrast, plasma MK4 concentration may be 
influenced by its tissue distribution and utilization as well as 
efficient recycling. 51,52) These differences may partly explain 
why a clearer association with WSI was observed for PK than 
for MK4.
This study had several limitations. First, the patients 
included in this study were already receiving stable warfa -
rin therapy, and their exact PT-INR values before warfarin 
initiation could not be confirmed. Consequently, WSI was 
calculated assuming a pretreatment PT-INR of 1.00. However, 
because patients with liver cirrhosis or liver cancer, which may 
affect baseline coagulation status, were excluded, substantial 
elevation of PT-INR before warfarin initiation was considered 
unlikely. Second, the present study had limited power to eval -
uate interactions between low plasma PK status and genetic 
or clinical variables because of the small number of patients 
with low plasma PK concentrations and the limited sizes of 
the relevant genotype subgroups. Therefore, the observed 
association between low plasma PK concentration and warfa -
rin sensitivity should be interpreted as an average association 
across the study population, and whether this association 
differs according to genetic or clinical characteristics remains 
unclear. Furthermore, the interaction estimates obtained 
from the present cohort were imprecise, precluding a reliable 
estimation of the sample size required for future interaction 
analyses. Future studies with larger cohorts and prespecified 
interaction hypotheses are required to formally assess poten -
tial effect modification. Third, daily dietary VK intake was 
neither assessed nor controlled, and plasma concentrations of 
menaquinones other than MK4 and the composition of the gut 
microbiota were not evaluated. Because plasma PK concentra -
tion may be influenced by recent dietary VK intake, the extent 
to which dietary intake contributed to the observed plasma 
PK concentrations could not be determined. Furthermore, 
because the gut microbiota produce several menaquinones 
other than MK4, 54,55) t h e  p o t e n t i a l  e ff e c t s  o f  g u t  m i c r o b i o t a - 
derived menaquinones on warfarin sensitivity remain unclear. 
Fourth, this study analyzed the quinone form of VK, which is 
stable in blood. Ideally, the hydroquinone form of VK, which 
serves as the reduced cofactor for GGCX, 4,7,48) should also 
be evaluated. However, this form is chemically unstable and 
readily oxidized during sample handling, 56) making accurate 
quantification using conventional analytical techniques diffi -
cult. Future studies should therefore establish reliable methods 
for quantifying the hydroquinone form of VK and investigate 
the relationship between VK hydroquinone concentrations and 
coagulation activity, which may provide more direct insight 
into the role of VK status in warfarin sensitivity.
Plasma PK and MK4 concentrations were not signifi -
cantly correlated with warfarin sensitivity when analyzed 
as continuous variables. However, prediction modeling and 
correction–effect analysis indicated that low plasma PK 
concentration, particularly PK <0.20 ng/mL, provided addi -
tional information for WSI prediction. In multivariable linear 
regression analysis, plasma PK concentration <0.20 ng/mL 
was independently associated with higher WSI after adjust -
ment for established clinical and genetic factors, whereas 
MK4-based models showed weaker and less consistent con -
tributions. These findings suggest that direct measurement of 
plasma PK concentration may provide additional information 
for understanding interindividual variability in warfarin 
sensitivity beyond that explained by genetic polymorphisms 
alone. In particular, plasma PK measurement may help char -
acterize increased warfarin sensitivity in patients with sus -
pected low VK status, such as those with poor dietary intake 
or nutritional deficiency. Further studies are needed to vali -
date the clinically relevant range of plasma PK concentrations 
during warfarin therapy, including the exploratory <0.20 ng/
mL threshold identified in this study, and to establish strate -
gies for safely managing patients with markedly low plasma 
PK concentrations.

[PMID 39356590 | PMC11424055 full text via pmc_xml] Comparative performance of pharmacogenetics-based warfarin dosing algorithms in Chinese population: use of a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model to explore dosing regimen through clinical trial simulation. :: Warfarin is a classic oral anticoagulant to prevent and treat thromboembolic conditions such as deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, atrial fibrillation, and mechanical heart valve replacement [1–3]. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), such as dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, and betrixaban, have seen increased use in recent years. Warfarin, however, has decades-long track record in clinical use and is still the anticoagulant of choice from a cost perspective. For patients receiving mechanical heart valve replacement, warfarin remains the first-line therapy as recommended by clinical guidelines [2]. Although warfarin is highly effective in reducing thromboembolic events, it is also one of the most common causes of serious adverse drug reactions due to large variability in dosing requirements [4]. Genetic polymorphisms in CYP2C9 (variant alleles: CYP2C9*2, 430C > T, rs1799853; CYP2C9*3, 1075A > C, rs1057910) and vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1 variant allele: -1639G>A, rs9923231) can account for up to 30–40% of dose variability [5,6]. Clinical factors such as age, body surface area (BSA), amiodarone use, smoking status, ethnicity, and so forth can account for an additional 20%, making for a total of 50–60% of dose variability due to genetic and clinical factors combined.
In clinical settings, routine monitoring of the international normalized ratio (INR) is typically used to adjust dosing and help maintain within the therapeutic range (INR of 2.0–3.0). Furthermore, pharmacogenetic dosing algorithms based on multiple linear regression relationships between maintenance dose and patient factors (clinical and genetic) have been developed to guide the dosing of warfarin. The Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) has recommended algorithms developed by the International Warfarin Pharmacogenetics Consortium (IWPC) and by Gage et al. for this purpose [7,8]. The use of pharmacogenetic dosing algorithms in clinical trials enrolling patients on warfarin for anticoagulation led to a higher percentage of time in the therapeutic range (%TTR) and reduced the combined risk of major bleeding, INR greater than 4, venous thromboembolism, or death as compared to clinically guided dosing [9,10]. Interestingly, in the Clarification of Optimal Anticoagulation through Genetics (COAG) study, there was an unexpected finding that African American patients on the pharmacogenetic algorithm by Gage et al. had lower %TTR compared to those on the clinical algorithm [11]. This was not observed in European patients, suggesting that the application of pharmacogenetic algorithms derived largely from European patient data can lead to differences in performance between ethnic groups. paragraphs.text: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 polymorphisms are the primary genetic determinants of warfarin pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, collectively explaining approximately 21% of dose variability seen in children (23, 24). The CYP2C9 polymorphisms CYP2C9*2 and CYP2C9*3 result in decreased warfarin clearance and thus lower dose requirements to achieve therapeutic effect (25, 26). VKORC1 encodes vitamin K epoxide reductase. The common promoter polymorphism in VKORC1 refers to a single-nucleotide variant (−1639G > A), which affects the hepatic mRNA expression. VKORC1 A-allele carriers have reduced gene expression and lower warfarin dose requirements and, together with CYP2C9 variants, VKORC1 genotype significantly influences warfarin maintenance dose, time to therapeutic INR, and risk of over-anticoagulati

The 2017 CPIC guideline update identifies the genetic variants CYP2C9, VKORC1, CYP4F2 and rs12777823 as key determinants of warfarin dose requirements and provides genotype-guided dosing recommendations for adults and children that integrate genetic and clinical factors (30). It is important to note that maintaining therapeutic drug monitoring with INR is necessary, regardless of genotype, as non-genetic factors (e.g., diet) remain important (30).

Pediatric cardiology patients use warfarin, an oral anticoagulant, for a variety of indications, such as prophylaxis in the presence of mechanical prosthetic heart valves, Fontan circulation, and Kawasaki disease associated with coronary artery abnormalities. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, impairing vitamin K-dependent activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. Warfarin is a racemic mixture and CYP2C9 metabolizes the more potent S-enantiomer.

paper_digests.summary: Paragraphs 8 and 9 establish that CYP2C9, VKORC1, CYP4F2, and rs12777823 are key genetic determinants of warfarin dose requirements in both children and adults. These genes significantly influence the maintenance dose, time to therapeutic INR, and risk of over-anticoagulation. Pediatric cardiology patients use warfarin for various indications, and CYP2C9 is involved in the metabolism of the more potent S-enantiomer of warfarin.

Warfarin has a large variability in dosing requirements that can be affected by clinical (e.g. age, BSA, amiodarone use, and smoking status) and genetic factors (e.g. CYP2C9 and VKORC1). Typically, an empirical approach is used in warfarin dosing, with an initial dose prescribed followed by at least weekly INR measurements and subsequent dose adjustments. The initial dose is usually based on population averages, such as 2–3 mg/d in the Chinese population, or in some cases loading doses may be prescribed during the first few days. The goal of making dose adjustments in the initiation phase is to help patients achieve and maintain within the therapeutic range (e.g. INR of 2–3). paragraphs.text: As noted in the FDA-approved lomitapide prescribing information, careful monitoring of LFTs and concomitant medication use are important considerations with the use of lomitapide. The patient’s transient and marked increases in LFTs associated with the use of a series of over-the-counter medications was instructive. Use of strong and moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors is contraindicated with lomitapide, and weak CYP3A4 inhibitors require a reduction in dose of lomitapide. Lomitapide may also increase exposure to statin, giving more cause for careful adverse event monitoring when initiating treatment11. paragraphs.section: Hematology and INR related adverse events during lomitapide treatment
paragraphs.text: Following approximately 129 weeks on study treatment, the patient was hospitalized for the management of hypovolemic shock, secondary myocardial infarction and congestive heart failure caused by a period of prolonged menorrhagia and attendant anemia (hemoglobin 5.6 g/dL, reference range 12.0–16.0). At time of admission her INR was 2.9, which was within her target therapeutic range. Despite investigating the etiology of the menorrhagia no clear diagnosis was evident. Progesterone therapy was initiated, and the patient’s bleeding resolved. During this time the patient missed one dose of lomitapide.

paragraphs.section: Hematology and INR related adverse events during lomitapide treatment
paragraphs.text: After 197 weeks of treatment, the patient was referred to the emergency department for evaluation of stroke symptoms in the setting of suspected viral illness, weight loss and an elevated INR of 5.0 (therapeutic target range 2.5 – 3.5). MRI of the brain identified small bilateral posterior fossa subdural hematomas, an acute punctate stroke in the left frontal lobe, and several areas of microhemorrhages. Her anti-coagulation management was stabilized and over time she experienced the resolution of neurological symptoms. Lomitapide was stopped during hospital admission and restarted at 20 mg/day approximately one month after her hospitalization, with the recommendation of frequent INR monitoring before and after each dose change. paragraphs.text: Background: Warfarin acts in heart valve replacement patients to minimize thromboembolic complications. We investigated whether patients can be distinguished based on their genotypes to efficiently and safely administer warfarin therapy after heart valve replacements.Research design and methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted in patients with warfarin therapy who underwent elective heart valve replacements between January 2013 and September 2018. The patients were divided into normal, sensitive, and highly sensitive bins based on their CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotypes. The primary endpoints were over-anticoagulation and overt bleeding.Results: 375 patients were enrolled, with 65 classified as normal, 281 as sensitive, and 29 as highly sensitive responders. [PMID 42876187 | PMC13669680 full text via pmc_xml] Reprocessing Mass Spectra from Therapeutic Drug Monitoring to Unveil Proton Pump Inhibitor Use and Quantify Phenoconversion of Escitalopram Metabolism in CYP2C19-Genotyped Patients. :: Study HighlightsWHAT IS THE CURRENT KNOWLEDGE ON THE TOPIC?Implementation of genotype‐guided drug dosing is one of the actions facilitating precision medicine. For some enzymes within the cytochrome P450 (CYP) family, for example, CYP2C19, genotype is a major predictor of metabolizer phenotype. For drugs metabolized by the respective enzymes, preemptive genotyping may predict dosing to the target plasma concentration range. However, in real‐world populations, there is a substantial genotype/phenotype mismatch, which reduces the validity of CYP genotyping in precision medicine. Multiple factors may underlie the mismatch between genotype and metabolizer phenotype, but comedication with drugs causing enzyme inhibition or induction is regarded as an important issue.WHAT QUESTION DID THIS STUDY ADDRESS?Escitalopram is one of the commonly prescribed antidepressant drugs showing large variability in treatment response, which is significantly attributed to genetic polymorphisms of CYP2C19, the major enzyme involved in escitalopram metabolism. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) exhibit CYP2C19‐inhibitory action to different degrees, so comedication may cause phenoconversion of escitalopram metabolism. Using an innovative high‐resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) method, we searched to unveil PPI comedication in therapeutic drug monitoring samples of escitalopram and quantify possible phenoconversion of escitalopram metabolism in a population comprising 2818 patients with known CYP2C19 genotype.WHAT DOES THIS STUDY ADD TO OUR KNOWLEDGE?Comedication with PPIs was disclosed in ~ 15% of the escitalopram‐treated patients. Significant phenoconversion of escitalopram metabolism was seen both for omeprazole/esomeprazole (most) and pantoprazole (least). In patients with genotype‐predicted rapid or normal CYP2C19 metabolism, comedication with omeprazole/esomeprazole caused escitalopram metabolism close to a genotype‐predicted CYP2C19 poor metabolizer.HOW MIGHT THIS CHANGE CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY OR TRANSLATIONAL SCIENCE?In real‐life clinical settings, information on comedications is required for successful application of genotype‐guided dosing. HRMS can effectively unveil interacting comedications in blood samples, which illustrate the innovative potential of this technology in translational and precision medicine.

Dabigatran is a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) used for the treatment of several thrombotic conditions. To date, very few pharmacogenetic studies on dabigatran were published. We aimed to investigate the influence of 59 polymorphisms in 15 genes (including CES1, UGT and CYP that encode enzymes and ABCB1 and SLC that encode transporters), concomitant treatment with pantoprazole and demographic characteristics (including sex or race) on dabigatran pharmacokinetics and safety. This was a candidate gene pharmacogenetic study. The study population comprised 107 volunteers enrolled in two dabigatran bioequivalence clinical trials; they were genotyped with a ThermoFisher QuantStudio 12K Flex OpenArray instrument. SPSS software v.21 was used for statistical analysis. Women showed a higher exposure to dabigatran compared to men. The concomitant treatment with pantoprazole was associated with a decreased exposure to the drug. CYP2D6 poor metabolizers (PMs) were related to lower clearance (Cl/F) (p = 0.049) and a tendency was observed towards higher area under the curve (AUC), maximum concentration (Cmax) and to lower volume of distribution (Vd/F) (p < 0.10). paragraphs.text: Study HighlightsWHAT IS THE CURRENT KNOWLEDGE ON THE TOPIC?Implementation of genotype‐guided drug dosing is one of the actions facilitating precision medicine. For some enzymes within the cytochrome P450 (CYP) family, for example, CYP2C19, genotype is a major predictor of metabolizer phenotype. For drugs metabolized by the respective enzymes, preemptive genotyping may predict dosing to the target plasma concentration range. However, in real‐world populations, there is a substantial genotype/phenotype mismatch, which reduces the validity of CYP genotyping in precision medicine. Multiple factors may underlie the mismatch between genotype and metabolizer phenotype, but comedication with drugs causing enzyme inhibition or induction is regarded as an important issue.WHAT QUESTION DID THIS STUDY

It is known that various PPIs exhibit different CYP2C19‐inhibitory potency. 16 , 17 Comedication with pantoprazole was identified in around 10% of the 2,818 included patients. paper_digests.title: The effect of CYP2C19 gene polymorphism on the eradication rate of Helicobacter pylori by proton pump inhibitors-containing regimens in Asian populations: a meta-analysis.

paragraphs.text: Premise: The effects of proton pump inhibitors (PPI) depend on metabolic enzyme CYP2C19 that has different activity due to gene polymorphism. The purpose of this meta-analysis is to determine the potential effects of CYP2C19 polymorphism on the efficiency of PPI-based treatment. Materials & methods: The PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, etc. were searched for relevant articles published in English or Chinese from inception to 31 May 2020. Finally, 26 randomized controlled trials and 15 cohort studies met the inclusion criteria and used for the meta-analysis via STATA version 15. Results: Poor metabolizer (PM) genotype Helicobacter pylori eradication rates were highest for Asian individuals receiving triple or quadruple first-line therapy based on PPIs (p < 0.05). paragraphs.text: Dabigatran is a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) used for the treatment of several thrombotic conditions. To date, very few pharmacogenetic studies on dabigatran were published. We aimed to investigate the influence of 59 polymorphisms in 15 genes (including CES1, UGT and CYP that encode enzymes and ABCB1 and SLC that encode transporters), concomitant treatment with pantoprazole and demographic characteristics (including sex or race) on dabigatran pharmacokinetics and safety. This was a candidate gene pharmacogenetic study. paper_digests.title: Effects of Genetic Polymorphisms of Cytochrome P450 Enzymes and MDR1 Transporter on Pantoprazole Metabolism and Helicobacter pylori Eradication.

paragraphs.text: Pantoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that is commonly used in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and metabolized by cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes CYP2C19 and CYP3A4. Pantoprazole is a substrate for multi-drug resistance protein 1 (MDR1). Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in CYP2C19, CYP3A4 and MDR1 affect enzyme activity or gene expression of proteins and may alter plasma pantoprazole concentrations and treatment success in PUD. In this study, we aimed to investigate the association between genetic polymorphisms in CYP2C19, CYP3A4 and MDR1 and pharmacokinetics of pantoprazole and therapeutic outcome in patients with either Helicobacter pylori-associated [H.P.(+)]-PUD or [H.P.(+)]-gastritis. paper_digests.title: Effects of CYP2C19, MDR1, and interleukin 1-B gene variants on the eradication rate of Helicobacter pylori infection by triple therapy with pantoprazole, amoxicillin, and metronidazole.

paragraphs.text: Eradication of H. pylori is an important treatment strategy in peptic ulcer patients. Current regimens of eradication consist of proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and two antibiotics. Effects of PPI may depend on their metabolism, and other factors important for the pathophysiology of peptic ulcer disease. Aim of the present study was to evaluate an association of CYP2C19, MDR1, and IL-1B polymorphisms with the eradication rate of H. pylori in Polish Caucasian patients treated with a triple therapy of pantoprazole, amoxicillin, and metronidazole. A total of 139 peptic ulcer patients, positive for H. pylori infection, were treated with triple therapy (pantoprazole + amoxicillin + metronidazole). paragraphs.text: The interaction between proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and clopidogrel in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients is mediated by CYP2C19 genetic variants. This study quantitatively assessed their CYP2C19 genotype-dependent impact on clopidogrel pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics using clinical data and physiologically based pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PBPK/PD) modeling. A total of 409 ACS patients from a prospective clinical study were genotyped for CYP2C19 (*1, 2, and 3 alleles) and evaluated for platelet reactivity index (PRI) following clopidogrel therapy, with or without concomitant pantoprazole or lansoprazole use. paragraphs.text: Assess the acceptance of genotype-based pharmacist recommendations made within a pharmacogenetics (PGx) clinic. The HLA-B*13:01 allele is a critical biomarker for dapsone- and cotrimoxazole-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs). Overcoming the limitations of centralized laboratory screening, we developed a portable electrochemical dual-sensing platform (EDP) for the simultaneous, ultrasensitive detection of HLA-B*13:01 alongside a TIMP-1 internal control. On screen-printed carbon electrodes (SPCEs), TIMP-1 is captured through robust biotin-streptavidin interactions, while HLA-B*13:01 relies on sequence-specific ssDNA hybridization. Crucially, the system utilizes methylene blue (MB) to precisely modulate both electrostatic repulsion and physical steric hindrance, enhancing signal discrimination. The platform demonstrates exceptional limits of detection, reaching 0.992 pg and 65.5 fg when evaluated by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and cyclic voltammetry (CV), respectively. Notably, accounting for genomic copy number, this corresponds to a practical detection limit of ∼3 HLA-B gene copies (1 × 10-2 ng genomic DNA), several orders of magnitude below conventional gel electrophoresis. Validated against 100 blinded clinical samples, the EDP achieved 100% sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy using ROC-derived cut-offs. By delivering a highly scalable, portable post-PCR screening tool, this work provides a high-performance alternative to standard methods, effectively mitigating SCAR risks and advancing the global accessibility of precision medicine.
[PMID 34630689 | PMC8495539 full text via pmc_xml] Comprehensive review on the pathophysiology, clinical variants and management of pemphigus (Review). :: Pathophysiologically, intraepidermal blistering diseases represent a group of disorders in which the body wrongly attacks healthy tissue with autoantibodies that attach to structural proteins in the mucous membranes and skin, which are components of desmosomes (desmocollins, desmogleins, plakins), causing intraepithelial blisters (1-3). This category of intraepidermal blistering diseases includes pemphigus, which can be classified into the following four entities: pemphigus vulgaris (PV), pemphigus foliaceus (PF), paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP), IgA pemphigus (subcorneal pustular dermatosis and intraepidermal neutrophilic IgA dermatosis).
The specific symptoms and severity of these diseases vary from one person to another, even among individuals with the same disorder. The diagnosis of bullous skin diseases is based on the typical skin manifestations, which may be objectified by Nikolsky sign and characteristic direct immunofluorescence (DIF) patterns in skin biopsies (1-3). The presence of specific circulating autoantibodies guides the diagnosis and allows a correlation between the levels of specific autoantibodies and the severity of the disease (4).
Since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, oral ulcerative lesions have been described, associated with SARS-COV-2 infection. Bullous dermatoses can arise with similar lesions in the oral cavity, which is why the clinical picture must be very well known (2-4).

The choice of drugs and their dosage should be based on clinical severity and patient comorbidities. Most patients require months or even years of immunosuppressive maintenance therapy. In other cases, untreated autoimmune blistering diseases can cause life-threatening complications (1-5). In recent years, new insight into the causes and development of these disorders has led to research into new therapies, such as the development of drugs that target the specific autoantibodies that cause the symptoms of these diseases (6).

paragraphs.text: This patient was homozygous for the NAT2*5B haplotype containing the nonsynonymous SNP 341T>C. This SNP leads to enhanced degradation of NAT2 and results in markedly decreased N-acetylation activity.32,33 The NAT2*5B haplotype has been associated with impaired biotransformation of isoniazid34 and, along with other slow NAT2 genotypes, is a risk factor for dose-dependent adverse reactions to sulfasalazine.35 These drugs share structural similarities with dapsone; however, NAT2 genotypes have not been previously evaluated in association with adverse reactions to dapsone. Because up to 18% of whites are homozygous for 341T>C (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/projects/SNP; rs 1801280), further work is needed to determine whether this genotype, or the larger NAT2*5B haplotype, confers risk for dapsone meth

Null mutations in the GSTM1 and GSTT1 genes have been associated with idiosyncratic toxicity from drugs such as the withdrawn oral hypoglycemic agent troglitazone36 and the cholinesterase inhibitor tacrine.37 A recent study of a patient with rash and arthralgia following TMP-SMX administration found a homozygous NAT2*5B genotype, as in our patient, and null GSTM1 and GSTT1 genotypes.38 Since GSTs are not involved in SMX disposition39 and have not been reported in association with dapsone clearance, we did not genotype for these null variants. However, it is possible that null mutations in either gene may have predisposed our patient to dapsone methemoglobinemia.

In conclusion, this patient developed methemoglobinemia on low prophylactic dosages of dapsone that are typically well tolerated. Genotyping revealed a homozygous slow NAT2*5B haplotype, along with low CYB5A and CYB5R3 expression and b5/ b5R reduction activity, but no evidence of rapid CYP2C19*17 genotype. Either or both of these pathways may have contributed to the risk of this adverse event, and further work will determine whether these detoxification defects confer risk for dapsone methemoglobinemia in the general population.

NAT2 activity was not evaluated, since this isoform is not expressed in peripheral blood.19 Another subject, a white woman with a history of sulfamethoxazole-associated skin rash, was also homozygous for the same 341T>C (Ile114Thr) allele (data not shown). The patient’s genomic DNA was resequenced at the CYP2C19*17 loci. The patient was homozygous wild-type for both −3402C and −806C (data not shown).

paragraphs.text: Dapsone is a drug used to treat leprosy. Dapsone causes a highly morbid and potentially fatal severe drug hypersensitivity reaction (DHS) in 1-3% of leprosy cases. The allele HLA-B*13:01 is a known genetic risk factor for DHS. However, resource-intensive genotyping methods preclude its testing in resource-limited settings. This study aimed to develop an endpoint PCR assay to detect the presence of HLA-B*13:01. DNA was extracted from blood samples of leprosy patients at Anandaban Hospital, Nepal (2022-24). A duplex endpoint PCR was optimized and validated against a previously validated commercial qPCR method and NGS (next‑generation sequencing).
